name: Supreme Court of Montana – Chief Justice Cory James Swanson
summary: In State v. Stroup, 2026 Mont. LEXIS 650 (Mont. May 8, 2026), the defendant’s attorney filed a motion to dismiss that the defendant claimed mistakenly contained “appended research and work-product materials,” which the court determined were “implie[dly] . . . prepared with the use of [GenAI].” The filing lacked the necessary GenAI disclosure required by Local Rule 3(g). After counsel filed a corrected motion with a proper certification, the trial court vacated the defendant’s trial date sua sponte, rejected all defense filings, and characterized the conduct as reflecting not only the “inept use of GenAI but also an unacceptable level of practice before this [c]ourt.” The trial court also “took judicial notice that [defense] counsel had allegedly filed documents in two other cases before him that similarly failed to properly disclose her use of GenAI in their preparation.” The defendant then petitioned the Montana Supreme Court to disqualify the trial judge, arguing that the judge’s response to the GenAI disclosure violation evinced personal bias. The Supreme Court denied the petition, holding that the trial court’s decision to “impose sanctions of a kind permitted under Local Rule 3(g), when counsel admittedly violated Rule 3(g) on numerous occasions involving at least three separate cases,” did not demonstrate personal bias or prejudice sufficient to warrant disqualification.

name: D. Colo. – Judge Nina Y. Wang
summary: In Coomer v. Lindell, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 128372 (D. Colo. July 7, 2025), counsel for the defendants included AI-generated citations in their opposition brief to the plaintiff’s omnibus motion in limine. During the final pre-trial conference, defense counsel admitted that they “ran [the brief] through AI” but “did not [cite] check” the result. Emphasizing that “Rule 11 applies to the use of artificial intelligence,” the court expressed skepticism that the incident was “simply an inadvertent error,” held that defense counsel violated Rule 11, and imposed joint and several sanctions of $3,000 on one attorney and his law firm, and individual sanctions of $3,000 on another attorney. Judge Wang declined to sanction the defendants themselves, however, as counsel “confirm[ed] that [he] did not advise” his clients that he used AI tools in his practice.Then, in Coomer v. Lindell, Civil Action No. 22-cv-01129-NYW-SBP, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 101691 (D. Colo. May 7, 2026), the court observed that the defendants included in their post-trial motions a citation that listed the incorrect court and did not support the proposition for which it was cited.  The court again ordered counsel to show cause.  In response, the attorney maintained that he did not use GenAI and that “the error was minor,” And that the “circumstances at issue here are not . . . the same type of AI generated error . . . that was the subject of that earlier sanction.”  The court disagreed that his error was not serious, attributing its pattern to a “form of hallucination that has already occurred in this case,” and reasoned that a greater sanction than previously was needed to deter this misconduct.  The court imposed a $5,000 sanction.

name: Supreme Court of Georgia – Justice Benjamin Arthur Land
summary: In Payne v. State, No. S26A0459, 2026 Ga. LEXIS 136 (May 5, 2026), the assistant district attorney included nine citations that do not exist or “do not stand for the proposition asserted” in her response to the defendant’s motion for a new trial. The court vacated the trial court’s order and remanded the case to the trial court for a new order that “shall not contain any fictitious or misattributed case citations” and “shall not be prepared by counsel for either party.”  The court also clarified its prior order and required counsel for the State to produce “all communications it had with the trial court concerning the proposed order denying [the defendant’s] motion for a new trial.”

name: Magistrate Judge Patricia D. Barksdale
judge: Chief Judge William Holcombe Pryor | Judge Kevin Christopher Newsom | Judge Andrew Lynn Brasher | Magistrate Judge Patricia D. Barksdale
summary: In Williamson v. TransUnion LLC, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 12852 (11th Cir. May 4, 2026), the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal with prejudice of the pro se plaintiff’s amended complaint as a sanction for his repeated misconduct. In front of the district court, the plaintiff cited nonexistent cases found through GenAI, misquoted and misrepresented actual cases, and continuously violated court rules and orders despite multiple warnings and show-cause hearings. At the district court’s second show-cause hearing, the plaintiff admitted that “some of the cases he cited did not exist, and that he had found them using [GenAI].” The magistrate judge found that the plaintiff’s errors were “‘some of the most egregious things’” she had seen from a pro se litigant and that she “had given him many chances to comply with the Local Rules and court orders.” The magistrate judge issued a report and recommendation finding that the plaintiff’s “repeated citation to nonexistent cases and misquotation and misrepresentation of cases and holdings, intentional misrepresentation of facts, and continuous violation of rules and court orders” warranted dismissal with prejudice, as “no lesser sanction would suffice.” Notably, in a post-judgment order, Williamson v. TransUnion LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 101962 (M.D. Fla. May 8, 2026), the magistrate judge observed that the plaintiff’s continued filings contained no citations to authority, suggesting he “continues to use [GenAI] to prepare the papers he files in this court, but now avoids citing non-existent cases by citing no cases at all.” The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the magistrate judge’s recommendation for dismissal, holding that the district court properly exercised its discretion under its “inherent power to manage its docket” and that the plaintiff’s misconduct was willful.

name: D. Utah – Magistrate Judge Cecilia M. Romero
summary: In Wilkes v. Canyons Sch. Dist., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 99436 (D. Utah May 4, 2026), the attorneys for the plaintiffs cited nonexistent cases in their amended complaint. The court found that counsel violated their “professional responsibilities under Rule 11(b) by failing to reasonably verify the existence and accuracy of the non-existent cases.” The court also noted that this was not the first time the same counsel had been admonished for improper GenAI use in this district.  As a sanction, the court ordered counsel to pay $7,000 to reimburse the defendants’ legal expenses, finding that the monetary sanction, combined with an outstanding CLE requirement from the prior matter, was “sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct by others similarly situated.” The court granted partial dismissal of the amended complaint on other grounds.

name: D.N.M. – Magistrate Judge Jerry H. Ritter
summary: In Carter v. Uzglobal LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 96883 (D.N.M. May 1, 2026), the attorney for the plaintiffs filed a response brief and two motions to compel that collectively contained sixteen hallucinated cases. The court found that an associate attorney at counsel’s firm had drafted the filings using GenAI, and that the signing attorney “reviewed” the briefs for “writing style, argument, etc.” but “did not verify the cases cited.” The court noted that opposing counsel had notified plaintiffs that they had cited an “unlocatable case” in April 2025, yet the signing attorney “proceeded to file the two compromised motions to compel in June” without reviewing her briefs until “alerted a second time by another attorney.” The court found that the signing attorney violated Rule 11, holding that “submitting documents with AI-hallucinated cases is objectively unreasonable” and that an attorney “cannot delegate her obligations under Rule 11.” The court imposed sanctions, but noted that the attorney “did not attempt to avoid responsibility,” “self-reported to the New Mexico state bar,” took a CLE course, and “offered to pay reasonable attorney fees.” As sanctions, the court ordered the attorney to self-report to the Texas state bar and disciplinary boards, to update her New Mexico state bar reporting with a copy of this order, and pay a $1,000 fine to the Clerk of Court, submit proof of attendance at an AI-focused CLE course. The court also permitted the defendants to move for an award of attorney fees and costs.

While the court found the appellant’s briefing “inadequate” and his “gross misrepresentations of the record and misstatements of the law” to be unacceptable, it nevertheless reached the merits of the appeal and affirmed the trial court’s order dismissing the appellant’s claims on other grounds.

name: S.D.N.Y. – Magistrate Judge Gabriel W. Gorenstein
summary: In Jimenez-Fogarty v. Fogarty, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 94006 (S.D.N.Y. The court ordered the attorney to show cause and to provide “a complete and detailed description of the process of the drafting of the two memoranda of law” and the role of “any individual or computer system” involved. However, the court observed that the attorney’s response “offers only airy generalities and conclusory statements” and “contains no coherent explanation for how the two memoranda of law came to contain the fabricated citations,” variously attributing them to “typographical errors, misreading of secondary sources, or limitations in the search functionality of legal databases,” after only later suggesting that LexisNexis’s “[Gen]AI-driven features . . . may very well have” generated them. The court concluded that the attorney “used a[] [GenAI] program that generated the fabricated citations” and “failed to check that these citations were genuine,” in violation of Rule 11’s requirements. The court found, by clear and convincing evidence, that the attorney “acted in bad faith,” citing the attorney’s “obdurate refusal to explain how the citations came to be included in her briefs,” her “complete lack of acceptance of responsibility,” and the fact that she filed additional briefs in other courts containing fabricated citations even after the court had issued its orders to show cause, including one in the Second Circuit that resulted in a referral to the court’s Grievance Panel. As sanctions, the court imposed a $2,500 fine under Rule 11, ordered the attorney to supply a copy of the opinion to her client, and directed her to alert the presiding judge in each pending case where she appears as attorney of record.

The court also admonished the supervising attorney—the firm’s namesake and principal—for failing to appear at the show cause hearing or file any response and ordered him to submit a declaration addressing his supervisory responsibilities. In a second order, signed on April 28, 2026, the court sanctioned the supervising attorney after he attested that he “did not conduct the research nor contribute to the drafting” of the brief and therefore did not believe the original order to show cause “was directed to” him, failed to appear at the first hearing, and failed to respond to subsequent orders until a further order to show cause was issued. The court held that “managerial and senior lawyers have professional and ethical duties to the Court, their clients, and their employees to appropriately supervise the work performed” and that the duty to check filings for accuracy “is nondelegable to other attorneys or to technology.” As sanctions, the court ordered the supervising attorney to circulate all show cause documents to firm staff, four hours of live, in-person CLE (two hours on supervision of junior attorneys, two hours on ethical use of AI), distribute the CLE materials firmwide, and to pay $1,001 in personal monetary sanctions to the court.

summary: In Fivehouse v. United States DOD, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 93026 (E.D.N.C. LEXIS 900 (Apr. 15, 2026), the pro se plaintiffs filed appellate briefs containing “copious citations to hallucinated authority” and references to “Centient AI,” some of which plaintiff “tried to obscure.” The defendant filed a motion for sanctions, to which the plaintiffs chose not to respond. The court initially struck the plaintiffs’ opening and reply briefs and gave the plaintiffs an opportunity to refile. Despite this second chance, the plaintiffs’ refiled briefs continued to rely on “unsupported arguments and illegitimate citations,” including “abundant citations to both hallucinated cases and fictitious holdings and quotations from existent cases.” The defendant filed a second motion for sanctions, which the plaintiffs again declined to address. Citing recent Illinois appellate authority holding that the “[f]lagrant and unprincipled use of [GenAI] without ensuring the accuracy of the generated response ‘is an abuse of the adversary system,’” the court found that the plaintiffs’ “persistent dependence on incoherent arguments, hallucinated authority, and fictitious case holdings has rendered review impossible.”  The court again struck the plaintiffs’ briefs, and then dismissed the appeal for failure to comply with Illinois Supreme Court Rule 341, which regulates both brief formatting and reliance on authorities.

name: Appellate Court of Illinois, Third District – Judge Matthew G. Bertani
court: Appellate Court of Illinois, Third District
summary: In Hulvat v. Gumina, 2026 IL App (3d) 240628-U, 2026 Ill. App. Unpub. LEXIS 869 (Apr. 9, 2026), the pro se plaintiff included “citations to nine nonexistent cases” in his initial appellate brief. In response to the court’s order to show cause, the plaintiff admitted that the errors were the result of GenAI. Nevertheless, he argued that the court should not impose sanctions because he is self-represented, relied in good faith on “a well-known [GenAI] legal research tool” and corrected his error by filing an amended brief. The court disagreed, reasoning that citing to nonexistent cases constitutes a willful violation of Illinois Supreme Court Rule 375(a) and allows for sanctions. The court also cited Rule 375(b), which permits a reviewing court, in its discretion, to impose punitive sanctions for filing a frivolous appeal, including where a party cites fictitious cases. The court declined to strike the plaintiff’s brief and dismiss his appeal, but found that monetary sanctions were appropriate, ordering the plaintiff to pay the defendants’ appellate attorney fees (calculated as $3,178) incurred in discovering and addressing the errors. The court noted that further sanctions could have been appropriate, but that it found the award of fees sufficient for deterring similar conduct. The court affirmed the circuit court’s judgment on other grounds.

name: Superior Court of Guam – Judge Elyze M. Iriarte
summary: In Hocog v. Cook-Huynh, 2026 Guam Trial Order LEXIS 46 (Super. Ct. Guam Apr. 7, 2026), the defendant’s counsel included “at least thirteen . . . incorrect statutory citations, case cites, and quotes, plus misattributions and a fake case” in the defendant’s motion to dismiss.  In response to the order to show cause, counsel maintained that the errors were “clerical,” that he accidentally filed a draft brief, and that his secretary failed to correct the draft.  Although he also “acknowledged his ultimate responsibility, stressed the errors were inadvertent, and noted steps to prevent future issues,” the court noted that he offered “no further explanation” for the ficticious citations and instead only proposed corrective measures “focused . . . on preventing the filing of outdated drafts.”  The court concluded that counsel used GenAI without “adequate human verification,” violated the Guam Rules of Professional Conduct, and violated Guam Rule of Civil Procedure 11.  In imposing sanctions, the court considered the fact that this was counsel’s first violation and that there have been no similar cases in Guam yet.  Judge Iriarte also considered that counsel “repeatedly blamed his secretary before conceding ultimate duty” and that the “repeated minimization of AI errors in what amounts to 42% of his citations in that document” undermines his assertion that he showed “full respect and candor” to the court.  The court determined that counsel’s actions were a “breakdown in the basic obligation to verify authorities before submission” and imposed a $1,500 sanction.

name: S.D. Ala. – Judge Terry Fitzgerald Moorer
summary: In Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condo. Owners Ass'n, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 70410 (S.D. Ala. Mar. 31, 2026), the attorney for plaintiffs filed multiple pleadings in a condominium dispute that contained fabricated citations and false statements of law, were discovered by both the court and defendants. The court issued two show cause orders detailing the misstatements and directing counsel to provide copies of the allegedly fabricated authorities or a sworn declaration explaining how they were generated, but counsel’s responses were untimely, failed to fully address the court’s concerns, and “raised additional issues.” Although counsel denied using GenAI, he attached hundreds of pages of output from CoCounsel (Westlaw’s a legal AI research service), that the court found “riddled with erroneous information” and described as “gibberish.” Counsel appeared at the first show cause hearing “woefully unprepared” to address the court’s concerns and then repeatedly sought continuances, citing health issues, before ultimately refusing to attend the rescheduled hearing despite the option to appear remotely. Finding that counsel’s pattern of conduct—including fabricated citations, misrepresentations, failure to correct errors after notice, and refusal to participate in the sanctions process—amounted to bad faith, the court sanctioned counsel under Rule 11, Alabama Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3 (the Alabama professional rule analogue to Rule 11), and its inherent authority. The court imposed a public reprimand requiring counsel to file the order in all active and future cases for twelve months, ordered counsel to pay $55,597.00 in attorney fees to defense counsel, referred the matter to the Alabama State Bar with a recommendation that counsel “be found incompetent to practice law,” and directed the order submitted for publication in the Federal Supplement.

name: D. Ariz. – Senior Judge Grant Murray Snow
summary: In Montes v. Suns Legacy Partners LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 68888 (D. Ariz. Mar. 31, 2026), the defendant moved for Rule 11 sanctions against the attorneys for plaintiff after identifying at least eighteen instances of fictitious citations or fabricated quotations across four filings. The court found that the citations had “all the markings of a hallucinated case created by [GenAI] tools” and that counsel failed to conduct a “reasonable and competent inquiry” into the existence of the fabricated authorities. Counsel never took responsibility, instead attributing the errors to a law clerk, a LexisNexis cite-checking tool, “formatting” or “clerical” errors, and even to a “profound lack of diligence” by opposing counsel. The court rejected these explanations, noting that counsel’s Rule 11 obligations cannot be delegated and that running a brief through a cite-checking tool is no substitute for actually reading the cited cases. Finding that counsel’s conduct was not objectively reasonable, the court ordered both attorneys and their respective law firms, jointly and severally, to pay the defendant’s reasonable attorney fees incurred in discovering the fabricated authorities and briefing the sanctions motion. The court further ordered counsel to serve a copy of the order on their client, complete a CLE course on the ethical use of AI in law practice, and directed the Clerk to serve the order on the relevant state bars and on all judges in the district. The court granted in part and denied in part the defendant’s motion to dismiss and denied the motion to strike on other grounds.

summary: In Williams v. Crystal Springs Apts. LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 67113 (D. Ariz. Mar. 30, 2026), the court addressed the pro se plaintiffs’ use of GenAI tools to draft their amended complaint in ruling on the plaintiffs’ application for leave to proceed in forma pauperis. Though the plaintiffs’ original complaint included a disclosure that certain AI tools were used for drafting purposes and confirmed that factual allegations were based on the plaintiffs’ “personal knowledge and documentation,” the amended complaint contained no such disclosure (despite appearing to have been drafted using AI as well), “[did] not establish any plausible basis for relief[,] and assert[ed] claims that are not recognized under existing law.” The court reminded the parties that GenAI tools are not prohibited but must be used with caution. As such, Judge Lanham ordered the plaintiffs to include a “separate declaration” attached to all future filings where “Generative AI” is used, in which the plaintiffs must (i) confirm that the filing was independently “reviewed and verified;” and (ii) identify the portion(s) that “incorporate[] [GenAI] outputs. The court warned that any party who submits a filing with “inaccurate or undeclared generative AI outputs” could face sanctions. The court ultimately dismissed the plaintiffs’ amended complaint “with limited leave to amend.”

name: D. Mass. – Judge Margaret R. Guzman
summary: In Souza v. City of Fitchburg, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 67397 (D. Mass. name: D. Or. – Magistrate Judge Stacie F. Beckerman
summary: In Fleck v. Del-One Fed. Credit Union, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 67368 (D. Or. Mar. 30, 2026), the pro se plaintiff filed a response to the defendant’s motion to dismiss that contained misquoted local rules and a citation to a nonexistent case. The plaintiff had previously acknowledged using his company’s AI “systems” to “prepar[e] and format[]” his complaint and exhibits. The court confirmed that the purported citation “does not generate a case” and that the only source on Westlaw containing the purported quotation was the plaintiff’s own filing, noting that the plaintiff's “implicit invitation to make ‘findings’ that ‘mirror[]’ a hallucinated case” lent “further support” to the court’s assumption that the plaintiff used GenAI. Citing recent authority regarding GenAI hallucinations in litigation, the court reminded the plaintiff that Rule 11 requires all litigants to “read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the legal authorities on which they rely,” and that relying on fabricated opinions “is an abuse of the adversary system.” The court warned that any further hallucinated legal citations will expose the plaintiff to sanctions. name: 3d Cir. – Judge Peter Phipps, Cindy Kyounga Chung, and Jane R. Roth (dissenting in part)
judge: Judge Peter Phipps | Judge Cindy Kyounga Chung | Judge Jane R. Roth
summary: In McCarthy, P.A. v. United States DEA, No. 24-2704, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 9000 (3d Cir. Mar. 27, 2026), the appellant’s counsel “relied on case overviews generated by AI and provided to him by a non-attorney . . . without verifying the existence or accuracy of the citations” for his opening brief. The Government noted the “factual and legal inaccuracies” in its response brief. The appellant’s counsel then failed to check the citations in his Reply Brief, characterizing erroneous citations as “a good faith effort to chronicle Agency disparities, [and that there were] some immaterial misstatements about the cited cases' tangential details.” In response to the court’s order to provide copies of the cases, the appellant’s counsel “disclosed, for the first time, that the seven summaries were inaccurate and that one authority was hallucinated by AI,” and admitted that he first suspected GenAI use months earlier. The court ordered counsel to show cause. After a hearing, the court found that the attorney violated his duty to provide competent representation to a client under Pa. R.P.C. 1.1. In considering sanctions, the court found that the attorney’s apologies and corrective measures were mitigating factors, along with the fact that the court had “not yet addressed the failure of attorneys to use AI with appropriate guardrails” and that it did not specifically ask the attorney to address the rule. The court imposed a sanction of reprimand, involving notifying “‘all other courts before whom [Attorney] is admitted to practice and the National Disciplinary Data Bank of this discipline’ and provide them with a copy of the opinion imposing this discipline.” The court noted that it would have imposed monetary sanctions had this not been the first opportunity to address GenAI use. In a dissenting opinion, Judge Roth wrote that this case called for more severe sanctions because of the multiple instances of sanctionable conduct, the fact that the attorney received early notice of his mistakes, and that the court should not have to “explicitly forewarn against improper AI use” when it falls within existing legal rules.

summary: In Shaltry v. Benzing, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 66498 (E.D. Mich. summary: In State Nat'l Ins. Co. v. Treadwell, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 72098 (N.D. Ala. name: D. Or. – Magistrate Judge Mark D. Clarke
summary: In Couvrette v. Wisnovsky, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 60329 (D. Or. Mar. 23, 2026), the court imposed sanctions on the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs’ attorney for filing three briefs containing fabricated cases and quotations, which the court held constituted violations of Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and local rules. The plaintiffs continued to cite to nonexistent cases after the defendants called the errors to their attention and suggested GenAI misuse. In response to the defendants’ motion for sanctions, the plaintiffs simply deleted the non-existent citations and quotation marks while leaving the fabricated legal contentions unchanged. Plaintiffs argued that “[t]he inclusion of inaccurate citations was inadvertent and the result of reliance on an automated legal citation tool” and that they had taken proper corrective action. Defendants then re-filed their motion for sanctions. At the sanctions hearing, the court found that the plaintiffs failed to take corrective action and instead “attempted a coverup,” violating Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and the Oregon Rules of Professional Conduct. The court also found the plaintiff himself was likely the person using GenAI to draft and “share[d] responsibility [with his counsel] for the use of non-existent cases and fabricated quotations,” thus warranting sanctions against the plaintiff as well. As sanctions, the court struck without leave to refile plaintiffs’ summary judgment briefing; vacated the order allowing former local counsel to withdraw and ordered him show cause why he should not be subject to sanctions; assessed plaintiffs’ counsel a $15,000 fine to be paid to the clerk of court; requested defendants submit a bill of costs and reasonable attorney fees associated with their response to the fraudulent citations; and dismissed the plaintiffs’ claims with prejudice. In a later order, the court accepted defendant’s attorneys’ fees as reasonable, and ordered plaintiffs’ counsel and local counsel to pay defendants attorney fees totaling $94,704.38. Local counsel was ordered to pay $14,205.66, and plaintiffs’ counsel was ordered to pay the remaining $80,498.72.

summary: In Gentry v. Thompson, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 58718 (E.D. La. After the court issued an order to show cause, the primary drafting attorney appeared and admitted to using ChatGPT to find supporting caselaw and conceded that he neither checked the citations nor read the cited cases before filing. His supervising attorney acknowledged that he reviewed and revised other sections of the memorandum but failed to verify the hallucinated citations. The court found three attorneys whose names were on the filing violated Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 by failing to conduct a reasonable inquiry into the legal authority cited in the brief. The court sanctioned the drafting attorney $250 and his supervising attorney $1,000, reasoning that the supervisor bore greater responsibility given his roughly thirty years of experience and his duty to ensure the accuracy of filings by attorneys under his supervision. The court declined to sanction the Chief Deputy City Attorney but issued a formal admonishment, and the newly appointed City Attorney outlined remedial steps the office was undertaking, including a department-wide meeting and development of a written GenAI policy.

name: Neb. – Per Curiam (Justice Stephanie F. Stacy concurring)
summary: In Prososki v. Regan, 2026 Neb. LEXIS 38, 321 Neb. 38 (Neb. Mar. 20, 2026), counsel for the appellant in a dissolution of marriage appeal filed a brief containing numerous fictitious case citations, real cases with fabricated quotations and mischaracterized holdings, and fictitious quotations. The appellee moved to strike the brief and dismiss the appeal, asserting that the errors were the product of GenAI. Counsel denied using GenAI, attributing the errors to “sloppy” copying and pasting from Westlaw and having filed the wrong draft due to “a screen crack on his laptop,” but the court found this explanation “lack[ed] credibility” given the volume of fictitious quotations that could not be located anywhere in Nebraska jurisprudence. Noting that this presented a novel issue for Nebraska courts, the court held that the submission of fictitious authority, whether through GenAI or not, “can be resolved by application of [Nebraska’s] existing rules of professional conduct and court rules,” including the duties of candor toward the tribunal, competence, diligence, and good faith argumentation. The court struck the appellant's brief, dismissed his appeal, and referred his counsel to the Counsel for Discipline of the Nebraska Supreme Court.

name: Judge John J. Eklund concurrin
judge: Judge Eugene A. Lucci | Judge Robert J. Patton | Judge John J. Eklund
summary: In State v. Coleman, 2026-Ohio-965, 2026 Ohio App. LEXIS 988 (Ohio Ct. App. Mar. 20, 2026), defense counsel in a criminal appeal alleged prosecutorial misconduct by filing an application to reopen, in part based on allegedly “inflammatory, improper statements” by the prosecutor. That application contained fabricated transcript quotations, which defense counsel admitted was generated by ChatGPT, allegedly as a result of his paralegal using the tool without adequate supervision or verification. However, the purported quotes by the prosecutor were never made, which the court held impugned not only the prosecutor but also the trial judge (implying that the court permitted such improper statements). After the State identified the fabrications in its responsive filing and moved for sanctions, counsel neither withdrew nor amended the application, and subsequently appealed the denial to the Ohio Supreme Court without disclosing the fabricated content. Two months after the sanctions hearing, counsel filed a motion in an unrelated case that contained an embedded ChatGPT prompt in the text of the filing itself. And although counsel eventually proposed “remedial measures,” including the creation of an internal AI policy for his firm, that policy itself “bore the hallmarks” of having itself been generated by GenAI. Finding bad faith based on counsel’s familiarity with GenAI tools yet failing to verify citations, the significant nature of the hallucinations, and his failure to take corrective action, the court imposed comprehensive sanctions: a $2,000 monetary fine, referral to the Office of Disciplinary Counsel, a two-year requirement to serve the sanctions order on the presiding judge of every court in which counsel enters a new case, a two-year certification and verification requirement for all filings, six hours of mandatory CLE on AI ethics, striking of the fabricated application, removal as counsel, and written apologies to the individuals defamed by the fabricated filing.

Despite understanding the risks associated with GenAI use, including the potential for generating fabricated legal authority, the attorney admitted to “not fully vetting or verifying the governing law or the citations within the submitted memorandum.” The attorney took responsibility, acknowledged the seriousness of his actions, and informed the court that he had undertaken remedial measures, including enrolling in CLEs on GenAI-assisted legal practice and developing strengthened verification protocols. Citing the Fifth Circuit’s observation that courts are increasingly “burdened [with] addressing AI hallucinations in court filings,” Judge Edwards emphasized that a lawyer's duty remains “unchanged” regardless of whether GenAI is used, as the lawyer must “ensure that the legal propositions and authority generated are trustworthy.” While commending the attorney for his “candor, honesty, and the remedial measures he has undertaken,” the court found that these mitigating factors did not excuse the attorney’s conduct, as Rule 11 requires attorneys to verify the accuracy of submissions to the court at a minimum. The court imposed a $1,000 monetary sanction to be paid personally by the attorney.

summary: In In re Domestic P'ship of Torres Campos & Munoz, 2026 Cal. App. LEXIS 130 (Cal. Ct. App. Mar. 5, 2026), the court considered an appeal from a family court order and addressing respondent’s counsel’s citation to fictitious legal authorities in a letter sent to opposing counsel, in the respondent’s declaration, and in briefs filed with the appellate court. Respondent’s counsel admitted to citing non-existent cases, stating that one “may have” been generated by GenAI and that the other was sourced from a “Reddit article that was authored by a non-attorney blogger,” and that she “did not verify” those authorities. The family court then issued an order which relied upon those non-existent cases first cited by respondent (and then later cited by petitioner); the appellate court ruled it constituted an abuse of discretion for the family court to rely “in material part on fictional case authorities in rendering a decision or making an order.” However, the fact that the petitioner had also cited the fictitious cases and failed to identify them earlier (before belatedly raising them as grounds for reversal) constituted forfeiture of that claim of error. In addressing the GenAI misuse, the appellate court noted that—despite respondent counsel’s admission to citing the cases in question—she “doubled down” in her defense of the fake citations even when confronted with them by opposing counsel. The court found this conduct to fall “far short of [the attorney’s] duty of candor with the court” under California’s Rules of Professional Conduct and the Rules of the Court. As a result, the appellate court imposed $5,000 in sanctions on respondent’s counsel (as well as ordering her to report the sanction to the state bar), particularly because she both “persisted in and aggravated the misconduct” by defending the fictitious citations, and because she “still has not been entirely forthcoming” about how one of the citations was originally sourced.

summary: In Woodward Harbor L.L.C. v. City of Mandeville, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 45132 (E.D. La. The court had previously dismissed the plaintiffs’ complaint with prejudice for failure to state a claim, noting the numerous hallucinated citations and concluding they were likely the product of GenAI, and ordered the attorney to show cause as to why he should not  be sanctioned for the hallucinate citations. The court also declined to sanction three other attorneys whose names appeared on the brief (based on their declarations that the filing attorney bore sole responsibility for verifying the brief’s accuracy), but reminded them of their “personal, nondelegable responsibility” under FRCP 11.

summary: In Dixon v. Multicare Health Sys., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 44646 (W.D. Wash. summary: In in re Est. of Carey, 2026 Wash. App. LEXIS 418 (Wash. Ct. name: N.D. Ala. – Judge Anna M. Manasco
summary: In Rivera v. Triad Props. Corp., No. 2:24-cv-01802-AMM, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 74689 (N.D. Ala. Mar. 31, 2026), the plaintiffs’ attorney (and one of the name partners of the law firm) included fabricated citations in the plaintiffs’ response to the defendant’s motion to dismiss. The attorney tried to correct the error by emailing an “accurate” version to the court ex parte. The court ordered the attorney to file a sur-reply for the court to determine whether to issue a show cause order. In the sur-reply, the plaintiffs’ attorney admitted to GenAI use, but only in a “supplemental capacity” and with “attorney review.” However, the attorney failed to acknowledge many of the specific citation issues. The court then issued a show cause order for why the attorney and his law firm should not be sanctioned. The attorney filed a response claiming that the mistakes were caused by a “computer error” and that he quickly fixed them. At the show cause hearing, the attorney then “blamed the court staff for not uploading his ‘correct’ document,” blamed opposing counsel for “not asking follow-up questions,” and provided inconsistent explanations for the errors. The court noted that the attorney had previously submitted filings with nonexistent citations in a different case. The law firm responded to the order to show cause with an assurance of commitment to candor and explained that it immediately enlisted two associates to investigate the situation when it came to light. The firm explained that the offending attorney “took several steps to cover the true extent of the situation” and never informed the firm or his clients about the extent of the filing issue. The firm eventually removed the attorney as a partner and stated its commitment to developing corrective action. The court found that sanctions were proper under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and the court’s inherent authority, and that the attorney’s conduct reflected “intentional, repeated choices—not isolated lapses in judgment attendant to unreasonable haste or excusable neglect.” The court found that the law firm was also subject to sanctions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 because the firm did not have any “meaningful procedures or internal controls regarding its attorneys’ [GenAI use].” The court imposed sanctions including: 1) Suspending the attorney from the practice of law in Alabama for three months; 2) disqualification of both the attorney and the law firm from further participation in the case; 3) referral of the attorney to applicable licensing authorities; 4) payment by both the attorney and the firm of defendants’ attorney fees; 5) a public reprimand of both the attorney and law firm.

summary: In Fletcher v. Experian Info. Sols., Inc., No. 25-20086, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 4834 (5th Cir. In response to the order to show cause, the plaintiff’s counsel denied GenAI use, and asserted that she “relied on publicly available versions of the cases, which [she] believed were accurate.” The court did not find this explanation credible and asked for additional explanation. The plaintiff’s counsel then admitted to using GenAI, but only to “help organize and structure [her] arguments and to break up overly long paragraphs.” She attributed the inaccurate quotations to “‘paraphrased summaries,’ which she claims to have ‘mistakenly believed . . . reflected the actual language of the cases,’” but the court could not find such summaries. The court also concluded that because counsel “did not explain the steps she took to verify” assertions in her brief, the court “concludes that she took none.” The court therefore found that she use GenAI to draft her brief and failed to check it for accuracy, and thus imposed a $2,500 sanction under Fed. R. App. P. 46(c) and the court’s “inherent power to impose sanctions for abuse of the judicial process.” The court noted that “[h]ad [counsel] accepted responsibility and been more forthcoming, it is likely that the court would have imposed lesser sanctions.”

name: Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Div. 3 – Judge Mark Hanasono, with Judge Lee S. Edmon and Judge Rashida A. Adams concurring

summary: In EFD USA, Inc. v. Band Pro Film & Digital Inc., 2026 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 1114 (Cal. Ct. App. Feb. 18, 2026), the appellate court identified several “fabricated quotations and inaccurate descriptions of legal authority” in the appellant’s briefing. The appellant’s lead attorney had used a GenAI “consultant” to prepare a draft opening brief and later used an “unidentified ‘AI system’” to shorten the brief to meet the word limit, but failed to confirm whether the system changed any citations during that process. The opening brief contained several fabricated quotations from real cases, including a leading case cited for a proposition it did not address and a purported quotation that did not appear in the cited authority. The respondents’ brief identified the deficiencies, but the appellant failed to acknowledge or explain the inaccuracies in its reply. In fact, the appellant’s reply brief also contained at least two fabricated quotations. The court then issued an order to show cause why the appellant’s attorneys should not be sanctioned for pursuing a frivolous appeal. In response, the lead attorney accepted responsibility for the errors and attributed them to the GenAI system he used to shorten the briefs. The court emphasized that it is “a fundamental duty of attorneys to read the legal authorities they cite in appellate briefs” and that counsel “plainly” did not read the cases before filing. Finding that the fabricated citations violated the California Rules of Court, which require that arguments be supported “with citations to real (as opposed to fabricated) legal authority,” the court imposed a $900 sanction against the lead attorney alone, payable to the clerk of the court. The court noted that while the deficiencies were “similar in kind” to those in a recent case where it imposed a $10,000 sanction, they were “far less widespread.” The court affirmed lower court’s judgment on all grounds.

judge: Presiding Judge Gary L. Lumpkin | Vice Presiding Judge William J. Musseman | Judge Robert L. Hudson | Judge Scott Rowland
summary: The Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals adopted Rule 1.17 governing the use of GenAI in documents filed before the court, entitled “Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence.” See In re Addition of A New Rule to the Rules of the Ct. of Crim. Appeals, 2026 OK CR 7 (Okla. Crim. App. Feb. 18, 2026).  Rule 1.17 defines GenAI as “any type of artificial intelligence that generates content or data in response to a prompt or query by a user.” The rule requires that when GenAI has been “used in the drafting of any document for filing in this Court,” the party or their counsel must “ensure that any portion of the document produced or modified by [GenAI], whether in whole or in part, has been verified as accurate by a person responsible for the document.” Courts may issue sanctions (including, but not limited to, waiver of issues, striking documents, and contempt) for failure to comply. In adopting the rule, the court recognized GenAI's potential to “produce misinformation or even to hallucinate.” Presiding Judge Lumpkin specially concurred, emphasizing that a lawyer’s signature on any document constitutes a certification that “all citations of authority, and cases in the document are true and correct, and all quoted language is accurate and correctly referenced,” and that any document that proves to be incorrect in its use of legal authority “subjects the lawyer to sanctions and disciplinary actions.”

name: 18th Jud. Cir. Fla. – Chief Judge Melanie Chase
summary: Chief Judge Chase's Administrative Order No. 26-10, titled “Disclosure of Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Attorneys and Self-Represented Litigants,” requires attorneys and self-represented litigants appearing before the Circuit and County Courts of the Eighteenth Judicial Circuit to disclose the use of any GenAI tool in the preparation of pleadings, motions, memoranda, responses, proposed orders, or other court records. The order notes that such tools may generate inaccurate assertions or citations, and that the court “should not have to parse case citations and parentheticals to discern whether cases exist.” Filings prepared with GenAI assistance must therefore include a certification stating that all factual assertions, legal authority, and citations have been independently reviewed and verified for accuracy, and that the filer accepts full responsibility for the filing's contents. The order emphasizes that GenAI use does not relieve any party of the duty of candor to the tribunal, the obligation to independently verify all factual assertions and legal authority, or compliance with applicable statutes, procedural rules, and the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar. All GenAI-generated content is deemed the work product of the filing party. The order also prohibits the submission of fictitious, fabricated, or hallucinated content; reliance on GenAI-generated citations without independent verification; misrepresentation of GenAI-generated content as independently researched authority; and failure to disclose GenAI use as required by the order, noting that failure to comply may result in sanctions.

summary: In Virgil v. Experian Info. Sols. Inc., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 29090 (S.D. Ind. summary: In Amarsingh v. Frontier Airlines, Inc., 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 3928 (10th Cir. The court ordered the plaintiff to provide accurate copies of the suspect cases or explain how the fabricated citations ended up in her brief and to show cause why she should not be sanctioned. In response, the plaintiff admitted that she had used ChatGPT as a research and drafting aid, which generated the fabricated case citations, and acknowledged that she did not verify that the cases existed or that the quotations actually appeared in the cited cases. summary: In Khan v. NSO et al., No. 2:25-cv-11961 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 6, 2026), Judge Frimpong issued a resources document for the pro se plaintiff. The document notes that while the court does not restrict any party's use of AI, parties are reminded that AI “may output information that is false, inaccurate, or biased” and that it is the parties’ responsibility to “personally ensure the accuracy of any statements and representations made in the course of the litigation even if it has been generated by AI.” The court’s resources guide also directs the parties to the California State Bar's Practical Guidance on the use of AI.

name: D. Colo. – Judge Nina Y. Wang
summary: In Berg v. United Airlines, Inc., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 25650 (D.  Colo. Feb. 6, 2026), the court denied the pro se plaintiff’s motion for extension and motion for reconsideration of Judge Prose’s prior order denying the plaintiff’s motion to compel discovery. Both Magistrate Judge Prose and Judge Wang had previously warned the plaintiff that her “filings contained erroneous and hallucinated citations consistent with misuse of [GenAI]” and that further violations could result in sanctions. Despite the warning, the plaintiff’s motion for extension cited to nonexistent and misrepresented cases. The court denied both motions on other grounds. Judge Wang imposed a filing restriction to counter the plaintiff’s “untimely, duplicative, and noncompliant” filings. The restriction prevented the plaintiff from filing any further motions without leave of court before the court rules on the defendant’s motion for summary judgment or vacates the order, noted that it will not grant leave without a certification that the use of AI is in compliance with the court’s standing order.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Conn. – Judge Stefan R. Underhill
summary: In Davila v. Roblen, LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 24971 (D. Conn. Feb. 6, 2026), the court addressed the conduct of the plaintiff's attorneys who filed a brief containing quotes generated by GenAI from legal authorities that did not contain those quotes. The court noted that one of the attorneys in question had previously been sanctioned by the court for submitting filings with GenAI hallucinations. See Cojom v. Roblen, LLC., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 225325 (D. Conn. Nov. 17, 2025). The plaintiff's lead attorney admitted that he used a GenAI tool, failed to verify the citations it produced, and based legal arguments on the fabricated quotes. The court found that this conduct constituted a “negligent[] . . . [failure] to perform [his] responsibility as an officer of the court” and negatively impacted the client, opposing parties, and the court itself by depriving the client of arguments based on legitimate precedent and requiring opposing counsel and the court to contend with “arguments based on phony law.” Noting the lead attorney’s acceptance of responsibility and commitment to remediation, the court ordered that he complete three hours of CLE on responsible AI use and publish a written article on the topic. The court declined to sanction co-counsel (who had requested to file a “corrected version” of the erroneous brief without disclosing that GenAI hallucinations were the reason for doing so), concluding that her lack of candor was not “a false statement of fact or law.”
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: Ind. Ct. App. – Judge Paul A. Felix
summary: In Mutugu v. Kiaraho, 2026 Ind. App. Unpub. LEXIS 203 (Ind. Ct. App. Feb. 6, 2026), the court dismissed the pro se appellant's appeal due to his “significant noncompliance with Indiana Appellate Rule 46,” which requires appellate briefs to be both accurate and follow certain filing guidelines, and awarded the appellee attorneys' fees. The appellant's brief was “deficient and violate[d] Appellate Rule 46(A) in almost every possible way,” including hallucinated and inaccurate citations. Of the 21 legal authorities cited in the appellant's argument, 5 cases did not exist, and 11 of the remaining authorities were “incorrectly cited or described.” Judge Felix observed that given the appellant's “citations to ‘nonexistent legal authorities and to real legal authorities that have nothing to do with the propositions they purport to support,’” it was likely that the appellant used GenAI to draft his brief. The court noted that “[c]itations to fictitious, AI-generated authority is a growing problem nationwide” and that “[c]ourts have sanctioned both attorneys and pro se litigants for including them in briefs.” Because the appellant's noncompliance substantially impeded appellate review and his appeal was “permeated with meritlessness,” the court granted the appellee's motion to dismiss, denied the appellant's motion to amend his brief, and remanded for a determination of reasonable appellate attorneys' fees.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: S.D.N.Y. – Judge Katherine Polk Failla
summary: In Flycatcher Corp. v. Affable Ave. LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 23980 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 5, 2026), counsel for defendant submitted a brief containing at least thirteen hallucinated citations and eight faulty citations to caselaw that existed but did not stand for the proposition he claimed. When co-defendant's counsel alerted the attorney to these errors, he offered a convoluted excuse involving his use of CaseText, CoCounsel, and vLex for research and cite-checking, citing his lack of access to traditional legal research databases. After co-defendant’s counsel reported the attorney to the court, an order to show cause was issued. In response, the attorney filed a submission containing “conspicuously florid prose”, including extended quotes from irrelevant books of fiction, and a quote misattributed to a case when it came from an article discussing that case. Despite explicit warnings, the attorney then filed a proposed reply brief containing another nonexistent citation, which led to a sanctions hearing.At the sanctions hearing, the attorney was placed under oath and admitted to using various GenAI tools including vLex, Paxton AI, and NotebookLM, but “attempted to minimize his responsibility.” The court found that the attorney's AI misuse resulting in erroneous citations, exacerbated by his "insouciant approach to cite-checking," was done in bad faith, concluding that he knew or consciously avoided learning that the cases he cited were not warranted by existing law, and continuously presented to the court faulty, GenAI-created citations and briefs. The court weighed the five factors relevant to terminal sanctions, finding: (i) intentional bad faith; (ii) prejudice to the court and parties; (iii) a pattern of misbehavior rather than an isolated incident; (iv) failure to correct the misconduct; and (v) likelihood of future misconduct. Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 11, the court entered default judgment against the attorney's client, struck the defendant's filings, and granted leave for co-defendant's counsel to submit a fee application.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Utah – Magistrate Judge Cecilia M. Romero
summary: In Odunze v. Lake Effect, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 24146 (D. Utah Feb. 4, 2026), the court addressed an opposition brief filed by the pro se plaintiff. The court noted that the plaintiff cited to a case that the court was “unable to locate.” Magistrate Judge Romero admonished the plaintiff that “[i]f artificial intelligence technology is being used,” he must “be in compliance with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11,” which requires that legal contentions be warranted by existing law. The court warned that “[c]ontinued misconduct of this nature may lead to sanctions.” On unrelated grounds, the court granted one of the defendant’s motions and denied the other as moot.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: N.D. Cal. – Magistrate Judge Susan van Keulen
summary: In Rako v. VMware LLC, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232131 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 25, 2025), the pro se plaintiff’s opposition briefs to the defendants’ motions to dismiss contained various “inadvertent citation errors,” which he did not attempt to correct until nearly six weeks after the defendants flagged these errors in their reply briefs. Judge Van Keulen reminded the plaintiff that all parties, regardless of their status of representation, must ensure that all assertions are verifiable and accurate. As such, the court ordered the plaintiff to include a footnote corresponding to “each citation located through AI” in all future filings that confirms that the authority is real and accurate (i.e., “Located through AI; Checked.”). On February 4, 2026, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 23692, after observing the parties “weaponizing accusations regarding the use of AI” since her November order, the court imposed an additional requirement: all disputes over whether a party has properly used GenAI are now subject to the meet-and-confer and joint statement requirements that apply to discovery disputes under the court's standing order . Any disputes that cannot be resolved through good-faith conferral must be presented in a joint statement not to exceed five pages.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D.N.J. - Judge Evelyn Padin
summary: In Kabir v. WebMD LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 22400 (D.N.J. Feb. 3, 2026), the court addressed the pro se plaintiff's repeated non-compliance with filing rules and prior warnings about hallucinated citations. The plaintiff, who had filed numerous motions and voluminous submissions throughout the litigation, “repeatedly attempted to circumvent” applicable filing rules and directly contacted both the Chief Judge and the presiding judge in violation of the court's policies. The court revoked the plaintiff's electronic filing privileges and ordered the Clerk of Court not to docket any future submissions through the alternate document submission system. Judge Padin also noted that the plaintiff's opposition brief “relies on hallucinated quotations,” citing a nonexistent case, despite prior warnings that “[h]allucinated citations will not be excused” and that the court “may sanction Plaintiff for further uses of hallucinated citations.” The court reiterated its prior warning that hallucinated citations “will not be permitted under any circumstances.” Judge Padin cautioned that if the plaintiff continues to inappropriately rely on GenAI, he may be subject to a pre-filing injunction or other sanctions, and denied the plaintiff’s pending motion with prejudice.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Kan. – Judge Julie A. Robinson
summary: In Lexos Media IP, LLC v. Overstock.com, Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 258649 (D. Kan. Dec. 15, 2025), the court granted in part and denied in part the plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a corrected opposition to a Daubert motion after the defendant identified “nonexistent quotations,” “nonexistent or incorrect citations,” and “misrepresentations about cited authority” in the plaintiff’s original brief—errors the plaintiff attributed to counsel’s unverified use of GenAI. The court held that allowing substantive changes would function as an improper sur-reply and that Plaintiff failed to show excusable neglect under Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b), emphasizing the prejudice to the defendant and the waste of judicial resources caused by the defective filing. Citing recent authority warning that careless use of GenAI can waste resources and undermine credibility, the court declined to permit a “do-over,” denied any additions of text or authority, and struck the original response. The court ordered Plaintiff to file a corrected brief by December 19, 2025 that omits all nonexistent quotations, nonexistent/incorrect/inapposite citations, and misrepresentations about cited authority. On February 2, 2026, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20994, following the corrected brief’s filing, the court issued an order admonishing all five plaintiff attorneys and sanctioning four of them, imposing fines ranging from $1,000 to $5,000, revoking one attorney’s pro hac vice status and ordered him to self-report to the state’s legal disciplinary authority, ordering the managing member of the law firm to create a more effective GenAI firm policy, and accepting local counsel’s “voluntarily sanction[]” of not serving as local counsel for a year. The court declined to sanction the fifth attorney, the “most junior attorney on this matter,” as he had no responsibility to review his supervisors’ work.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: DeKalb Cnty. State Ct., Ga. – Judge Ana María Martinez
summary: In Am. Express Nat'l Bank v. Flippin, 2026 Ga. State LEXIS 185 (Ga. Cnty. Ct. Feb. 2, 2026), the pro se defendant filed an “avalanche” of GenAI-generated motions, notices, responses, and other filings in a debt collection case, totaling approximately sixty or more distinct filings since October 2025. The court had previously entered a standing order requiring any party who uses AI to disclose such use and certify that every citation has been verified as accurate, applicable to all parties including pro se litigants. Despite including certifications of compliance with the Standing Order, the defendant’s filings were “replete with manufactured arguments and hallucinations,” invoking both real cases that did not support the propositions for which they were cited and “fictitious authority pulled from thin air.” The struck the defendant’s motion to compel from the record after concluding that it was “based exclusively on two nonexistent cases.” Although the defendant admitted to having submitted nine fictitious cases in good faith, the court observed that his “torrent of filings continued with frivolous arguments and misrepresentations of the law, which are just as troublesome.” Because of the defendant’s pro se status and his good faith correction concerning the fictitious cases, the court declined to impose sanctions but warned that “future abuses in this Court or others may not be met with such lenience.” On unrelated grounds, the court entered judgment in favor of the plaintiff.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: N.D. Cal. – Magistrate Judge Susan van Keulen
summary: In her updated Standing Order for Civil and Discovery Referral Matters (N.D. Cal. Feb. 2, 2026), Magistrate Judge Susan van Keulen sets forth procedures applicable to civil and discovery matters before her court in the Northern District of California, including provisions governing GenAI use. The standing order provides that the signature of counsel or a self-represented party on any submission containing GenAI-generated content, including citations generated by GenAI, constitutes a certification that the signing attorney or self-represented party has personally verified the content's accuracy. The court will impute any errors by GenAI tools to the attorney or party whose signature appears on the document containing those errors. The order warns that the failure to verify the accuracy of submissions, particularly the accuracy of citations to law and evidence, may be grounds for sanctions. Further, the order requires counsel to maintain records of all prompts or inquiries submitted to any GenAI tools in the event those records become relevant “at any point.”

name: S.D. Fla. – Magistrate Judge Eduardo I. Sanchez
summary: In Smith v. Kreeger, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 22187 (S.D. Fla. Feb. 2, 2026), a pro se plaintiff filed a complaint challenging state court custody proceedings. The court observed that the plaintiff's complaint relied on “non-existent case citations that appear to have been generated by [GenAI].” The court warned that the plaintiff's “pro se status does not absolve [her] of the responsibility to abide by a duty of candor to the Court” and emphasized that sanctions against parties who submit fabricated citations, including dismissal, are not uncommon. On unrelated grounds, the court recommended the denial of the plaintiff’s motion.

name: D. Nev. – Magistrate Judge Nancy J. Koppe
summary: In Schaaf v. Nellis Auction Holdings, LLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 22121 (D. Nev. Jan. 30, 2026), the court addressed plaintiff counsel’s continued misconduct, including hallucinated citations in three briefs stemming from the use of GenAI. In declining to impose terminating sanctions, the court acknowledged that case-dispositive sanctions are reserved for extreme situations and distinguished this case from one in which the complaint itself contained potentially hallucinated factual allegations. The court explained that here, the defendants pointed only to incorrect citations in briefing that had already been addressed through the underlying motion practice. The court, however, admonished plaintiff's counsel for his “lapse in his duties as an officer of the Court,” warning that continued misuse of GenAI would result in serious sanctions, including “case-dispositive sanctions imposed on his clients,” monetary penalties, and referral to the state bar. The court concluded by denying the defendants’ motion for case-terminating sanctions, motion to strike, and motion to stay.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Mo. – Judge Matthew Thomas Schelp
summary: In Mills v. City of St. Louis, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 19989 (E.D. Mo. Jan. 30, 2026), the court suspected that the pro se plaintiff used GenAI in preparing filings, which “contained misquotations or misrepresentations about case law he cited and discussed” with the “egregiousness of these misstatements increas[ing] over time.” In response to the order to show cause, the plaintiff admitted to using “electronic drafting tools that paraphrase legal principles.” Judge Schelp concluded that the plaintiff violated Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 by submitting fictitious and misleading cases to the court, regardless of whether the plaintiff used GenAI. In determining the appropriate sanction, the court considered that the plaintiff “made numerous misstatements in multiple filings,” continued making false representations after the court put the plaintiff on notice, and is well-educated and thus “should have known better.” Judge Schelp therefore reasoned that an “admonition, reprimand, or censure” would not sufficiently deter plaintiff from repeating this conduct, so the court dismissed the action with prejudice.

name: E.D. Wis. – Judge Pamela Pepper
summary: In SEC v. Nantomah, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 18126 (E.D. Wis. Jan. 30, 2026), the court noted that the pro se defendant’s citations in his response to the SEC’s complaint “bear the hallmarks of generative artificial intelligence.” Judge Pepper reminded the defendant of his obligations under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and warned that future filings that “contain citations to nonexistent cases or that quote language that does not appear in a cited case—whether the document is AI-generated or not” may result in sanctions. The court granted the SEC’s motion to strike the defendant’s answer on other grounds.

name: Ind. Ct. App. – Judge Melissa S. Mattingly-May
summary: In Wilcox v. Gingrinch, 2026 Ind. App. LEXIS 29 (Ind. Ct. App. Jan. 30, 2026), the pro se appellants cited a “substantial number” of cases that “either do not exist or have nothing to do with the propositions they purport to support.” The court observed that the “pattern and nature of the citation errors in the [] brief strongly suggest the use of [GenAI] without adequate verification.” Furthermore, Judge May could not evaluate the merits of the appellants’ primary legal argument because it was based on fabricated authorities. The court therefore considered those issues waived, noting that “[h]ad the [plaintiffs] performed basic verification, the waiver we find today could have been avoided.” Because this was the appellants’ first infraction, Judge May did not impose sanctions, but cautioned that “the submission of briefs citing nonexistent authorities in future proceedings may result in sanctions.”

name: W.D. Wash. – Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright
summary: In Greene v. GSK PLC, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 17248 (W.D. Wash. Jan. 29, 2026), the pro se plaintiff cited “several authorities which do not support her proposition or do not contain the text which she quotes” in her motion for court-assisted service, leading the court to suspect GenAI misuse. Judge Cartwright reminded the plaintiff that she is bound by Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 which requires that “legal contentions are warranted by existing law…” and warned that she could face sanctions if she submits nonexistent authority to the court in the future. The court denied the plaintiff’s motion without prejudice on other grounds.

name: W.D. Wis. – Judge James D. Peterson
summary: In Mims v. Brown, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 23032 (W.D. Wis. Jan. 29, 2026), the court addressed filings by the pro se plaintiff that contained indications of GenAI use. The court noted that several of the plaintiff's recent filings had metadata in PDF files listing ChatGPT as the source and one document bearing the ChatGPT logo. Judge Peterson warned the plaintiff to “proceed with caution,” observing that GenAI-generated court filings “often contain inaccurate factual representations, 'hallucinated' citations to non-existent cases, or fake quotations.” The court emphasized that all litigants, regardless of representation status, have an obligation to “read their filings and take reasonable care to avoid misrepresentations, whether factual or legal,” and that failure to do so may result in sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11, “including dismissal of their case with prejudice.” Judge Peterson encouraged the plaintiff not to use GenAI to draft submissions to the court, noting that even when such documents do not contain misrepresentations, “AI-generated legal documents often appear formal and legalistic, but contain very little helpful substance.” The court advised that it would be more helpful for the plaintiff to explain his position “using simple, everyday language, even if the result is that his filing looks less like a formal legal document drafted by a lawyer.” Judge Peterson concluded by reminding the plaintiff that if he does choose to use GenAI, he must still review his documents before filing and ensure that the facts and the law are correct, as he remains responsible for the content of documents filed in court.

name: D. Colo. – Magistrate Judge Susan Prose
summary: In Berg v. United Airlines, Inc., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15973 (D. Colo. Jan. 28, 2026), the court suspected that the pro se plaintiff used GenAI in her Motion to Compel Discovery because it included citations to “seemingly nonexistent cases.” The plaintiff included such citations despite the fact that she had also “included an artificial intelligence certification with each of her motions,” and the court had warned her on “multiple occasions to either avoid using artificial intelligence or to very carefully review her filings in order to avoid this exact scenario.”  Magistrate Judge Prose did not impose sanctions but warned that she will consider recommending dismissal or other sanctions if the plaintiff repeats this behavior in the future
