name: D. Kan. – Chief Judge John W. Broomes
summary: In his Standing Order on Use of Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) in Preparing Court Filings (D. Kan. Jan. 28, 2026), Chief Judge Broomes reminds litigants that “AI tools can produce false statements of fact or law, including citations to fabricated or incorrect legal authority.” The court warns that “all lawyers and parties, including pro se litigants . . . . are responsible for the content of their own filings,” must verify all content “drafted or assisted by an AI tool,” and may not make or fail to correct “a false or misleading statement of material fact or law.” The court has discretion to require a party to include a sworn statements disclosing the extent of AI use and certifying personal verification of the filing’s contents. Violation of the standing order could result in sanctions.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Tex. – Magistrate Judge K. Nicole Mitchell
summary: In Walder v. Experian Info. Sols., Inc., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 34005 (E.D. Tex. Jan. 27, 2026), Magistrate Judge K. Nicole Mitchell recommended denying the pro se plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment in a Fair Credit Reporting Act case and warned the plaintiff about her citation to fictitious cases. The defendant pointed out in its joint response that many of the cases cited in the plaintiff’s motions either did not exist or did not support the plaintiff’s propositions, suggesting the citations may have been the result of GenAI “hallucinations.” The court confirmed that it was unable to locate any of the three cases the plaintiff cited in her motion. Magistrate Judge Mitchell reminded the plaintiff that Local Rule CV-11(g) warns litigants that GenAI “may produce factually or legally inaccurate content” and requires litigants to “review and verify all content” for compliance with Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. The court emphasized that filing papers with citations to nonexistent law is “unacceptable” and that a “fake opinion is not ‘existing law.’” In light of the plaintiff's pro se status and consistent with other courts' treatment of similar issues, the court declined to impose sanctions but warned the plaintiff that further citation to nonexistent cases and noncompliance with Local Rule CV-11(g) may result in sanctions, “including her pleadings and other papers being struck, filing restrictions, dismissal of her claims, and monetary penalties.”
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: N.Y. Sup. C. – Judge Linda Kevins
summary: In Cassata v Michael Macrina Architect, P.C., 2026 N.Y. Misc. LEXIS 325 (N.Y. Sup. C. Jan. 27, 2026), the plaintiff’s counsel alleged that the defendant’s counsel plagiarized a brief that itself was improperly drafted using GenAI. In response to the order to show cause why the defendant’s attorney, supervising attorney, and law firm should not be sanctioned, the law firm stated that the attorney no longer worked at the firm and the supervising attorney had “no indication” that the attorney’s “work was plagiarized or improperly relied upon by [GenAI].” He further stated that the firm conducted additional training on the importance of compliance with the GenAI provisions in the firm handbook. At the hearing, the defendant’s attorney denied GenAI use in research but “appeared sincerely sorry” and admitted that she “found a brief on Westlaw which she incorporated into her opposition without verifying the citations, quotations, and propositions of law.” The court found this unpersuasive, and concluded that “citing non-existent cases, quotations, and specific propositions of law for which they do not stand and/or do not support, is unethical and sanctionable conduct” regardless of GenAI use. The courts considered the defense attorneys’ apologies, request for a “redo,” and inexperience as an attorney, ultimately concluding that sanctions were still warranted. In determining the amount of sanctions, the court found that the defendant’s attorney failed to verify cited authority before filing her opposition; that the attorney, supervising attorney, and the law firm “failed to promptly correct the record once inaccuracies were discovered”; and that the firm and supervising attorney lacked proper oversight and safeguards to prevent further misconduct. The court fined both the attorney and supervising attorney $1,000 (payable to the Lawyer’s Fund for Client Protection) and awarded $8,000 in attorney’s fees payable by the defendant’s law firm. The court further ordered that the attorney serve a copy of the decision and order on the clerk of court and Lawyer’s Fund for Client Protection.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: 17th Jud. Cir. Fla. – Chief Judge Carol-Lisa Phillips
summary: Chief Judge Phillips’ standing order titled, “Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Filings” permits the use of GenAI to assist in preparation, research, drafting of pleadings and documents, filing, and discovery, but requires that all GenAI-generated information have “appropriate human oversight,” including “checking citations, verifying factual claims, and analyzing conclusions.” The order further requires that any filing prepared with GenAI assistance identify the specific tool used and include a certification attesting to their personal review and independent verification of the filing’s accuracy, noting that failure to do so could result in sanctions (as can the submission of “false or misleading AI-generated content”). The order also emphasizes that attorneys may use GenAI only to the extent they can reasonably guarantee compliance with their ethical obligations under the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar. The order reminds pro se litigants that they must be aware of GenAI's propensity to generate fictitious legal authorities and must ensure such citations do not appear in court filings.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting
Applies to AI Used for Research

name: E.D. Pa. – Judge Mark A. Kearney
summary: In Lifetime Well LLC v. IBSpot.com Inc., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 13363 (E.D. Pa. Jan. 26, 2026), the court identified a briefing “contain[ing] at least eight false case citation hallucinations generated by artificial intelligence” submitted jointly by out-of-state counsel and local co-counsel for plaintiffs. In response, the court issued a show cause order, after which both sets of counsel admitted lapses in diligence tied to GenAI use. The out-of-state counsel terminated at least three attorneys responsible for preparing the briefing in response to the show cause order on her own accord, an action the court criticized by stating, “[the senior lawyer] did not explain why she did not use this mistake as a lesson rather than a reason to fire the new lawyer.” During the senior attorney’s investigation of her subordinate’s behavior, she found that the junior attorney relied on Lexis+ AI and LexisNexis Protégé as their primary research tools. The court also noted the peril out-of-state counsel placed local counsel in by asking him to sign and file the motion without diligently checking its citations, while admonishing local counsel for failing to properly vet the briefing before submitting it to the court. After learning of the filing’s deficiencies, local counsel voluntarily took CLE courses related to GenAI, reviewed all recent decisions from the Third Circuit and other courts related to GenAI misuse, and made a new agreement with out-of-state counsel to allow for ample review time of all motions prior to future filings with the court. The court found that both attorneys violated Rule 11 by submitting false citations and quotations without independently verifying the authorities, emphasizing that the signing attorney remains the final auditor of all legal and factual assertions. As tailored deterrence, the court imposed a $4,000 fine on the out-of-state attorney personally and required remedial educational outreach (including providing a copy of the court’s memorandum and order, the out-of-state counsel’s new GenAI firm-wide policy, and a cover letter to both local legal organizations and justices from other courts to whom the subordinate attorney previously submitted hallucinated citations to). The court imposed non-monetary sanctions on local counsel in the form of similar outreach to a local bar association. The court declined to refer either attorney to their respective bar disciplinary panels, and reminded all attorneys to use caution when submitting authority to the court.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Md. – District Judge Deborah K. Chasanow
summary: In Future Field Sols., LLC v. Norstrand, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 12278 (D. Md. Jan. 23, 2026), the court addressed defendants’ request for a show cause order and sanctions premised on indications that plaintiff’s reply brief was drafted using GenAI (including “incorrect case citations, unusual grammatical errors, responses to arguments [not made], and false factual assertions”). In ruling on the motion, the court explained that no rule forbids GenAI, but emphasized that Rule 11(b) requires a reasonable pre filing inquiry and that submissions drafted with GenAI without appropriate verification are sanctionable, further noting that courts are more likely to impose sanctions “when a party doubles down” on denials “rather than accept responsibility for doing so at the first opportunity.” The court found plaintiff counsel’s response to the defendants’ request did not fully address the accusations and, by partially shifting blame to the client, suggested insufficient attorney oversight. Although the court declined to issue a show cause order and denied the sanctions request without prejudice, Judge Chasanow noted that the issue of sanctions may be revisited later if appropriate. On unrelated grounds, the court granted summary judgment to the third party defendant and largely to the counterclaim defendants, denied the counterclaim plaintiff’s cross motions, dismissed any remaining claims, and ordered the company to show cause why default should not be entered.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: N.D. Tex. – Magistrate Judge Renée  Harris Toliver
summary: In Olali v. Ampex Brands, LLC, No. 3:25-CV-1602-K-BK, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 37552 (N.D. Tex. Jan. 23, 2026), the court suspected that the pro se plaintiff prepared his filings using GenAI because he cited to nonexistent cases, but failed to disclose that GenAI use, in violation of local rules. The court noted that this conduct also violated Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. The court found that the plaintiff’s “filings—built on AI-generated cases that stand for legal propositions in direct contravention of actual case law—are ‘the epitome of baseless.’” Magistrate Judge Toliver recommended granting the defendant’s motion to dismiss with prejudice, in part based on the GenAI misuse, and warned that further violations may result in sanctions.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: Ga. Ct. App. – Judges Kenneth B. Hodges, Christopher McFadden, and John Pipkin concurring
judge: Judge Kenneth B. Hodges | Judge Presiding J. McFadden | Judge John Andrew Pipkin
summary: In Tolbert v. State, 2026 Ga. App. LEXIS 21 (Ga. Ct. App. Jan. 22, 2026), the court found the appellant’s brief rife with briefing defects, including reliance on irrelevant or overruled authority, quotations that do not appear in the cited cases, and material misrepresentations of the record. Although the court declined to make “factual findings here as to how or why [plaintiff] provided inappropriate authority to this Court,” notably not accusing him of misusing GenAI, the court concluded that “such misrepresentations exist and this appeal is frivolous as a result.” The court then ordered the appellant’s counsel to serve the opinion on his client and the State Bar of Georgia, file a certificate of compliance within ten days, and complete three hours of CLE on brief writing before filing any further briefs, warning that future violations may trigger contempt and jeopardize his authority to practice, and noting that monetary sanctions are not authorized in criminal cases. name: D. Ariz. – Judge Krissa M. Lanham
summary: In Mavy v. Comm’r of Soc. Sec. Admin., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 157358 (D. Ariz. Aug. 14, 2025), Magistrate Judge Alison S. Bachus found that an opening brief that was “replete with citation-related deficiencies,” including non existent and otherwise deficient authorities, suggested possible use of GenAI. Magistrate Judge Bachus ordered counsel to show cause under Rule 11. Counsel’s response described a two layer internal review process, but acknowledged widespread citation problems. Magistrate Judge Bachus concluded that “well over the majority” of the brief’s citations were fabricated, misleading, or unsupported and that counsel failed to conduct a reasonable inquiry, thus warranting sanctions, including revoking the attorney’s pro hac vice status, striking the plaintiff’s opening brief, and ordering the attorney to notify her client and various courts about her errors—while expressly declining to find subjective bad faith. On review, Judge Lanham held (see 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 5981 (D. Ariz. Jan. 13, 2026)) that, although counsel acted recklessly in failing to ensure citation accuracy, sua sponte Rule 11 sanctions require conduct “akin to a contempt of court” (typically necessitating bad faith or the equivalent), which was not met here. Judge Lanham emphasized that warnings about GenAI use had been issued, that a two-layer review occurred, and that after problems surfaced counsel investigated other filings and took corrective steps—facts consistent with recklessness rather than bad faith—so she vacated the Rule 11 sanction in part. However, to protect the orderly administration of justice, the court left in place the striking of the opening brief and revocation of the filing attorney’s pro hac vice status, which she concluded were justified on non-Rule 11 grounds given the impaired administration of justice caused by a filing “riddled” with citation errors.

Magistrate Judge Stafford observed that the use of GenAI when drafting legal filings “is a very risky practice,” as litigants remain subject to Fed. R. Civ. To the latter, Judge Behm reiterated that the fact that the plaintiff did not draft the specific filings does not absolve her of her duty under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. Furthermore, the court expressed concern that reducing or eliminating the monetary sanction for the plaintiff will cause her to “misunderstand the seriousness of her conduct.” Judge Behm noted that the plaintiffs immediately followed the Magistrate Judge’s warning “with the very conduct they were warned about,” increasing the court’s doubt that a nominal penalty would deter the wrongful conduct.

name: D.S.C. – Judge Sherri A. Lydon
summary: In Cherleatha B. v. Bisignano, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 266530 (D.S.C. name: S.D.N.Y. – Magistrate Judge Gary Stein
summary: In Brian NG v. Amguard Ins. Co., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 266712 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 29, 2025), the pro se plaintiff cited to a case that “does not appear to exist” to support his “argument as to liability for insurance agents for their individual torts.” Magistrate Judge Stein warned the plaintiff that “[s]ubmitting fake citations to a court is unacceptable” and that future submissions with nonexistent citations may result in sanctions. The court also reminded all parties of Judge Broderick’s recent update to the Individual Rules and Practices in civil cases, which clarified that all parties, regardless of pro se status, must disclose the use of GenAI tools “in the preparation of any documents filed with the Court” and verify the documents’ accuracy, “including all citations.”  Judge Stein granted the defendants’ motion to vacate the clerk’s certificate of default on other grounds.

The court also reminded the parties that by presenting a filing, a party certifies that legal contentions are warranted by existing law, noted that fabricated opinions are not “existing law,” and emphasized that self-represented litigants remain bound by Rule 11’s obligations and potential sanctions. name: N.D.N.Y. – Judge Mae A. D’Agostino
summary: In Smith v. Smith, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 263592 (N.D.N.Y. Dec. 22, 2025), the court found that the plaintiff’s objections and reconsideration briefing bore a “distinctive style and syntax” characteristic of AI and relied on fictitious or mis-cited authorities, attributing the errors to GenAI “hallucinations.” The court adopted the magistrate judge’s report and recommendation, which recommended that (1) the plaintiff's complaint be dismissed with prejudice as to the plaintiff's constitutional claims against certain defendants; (2) the complaint be dismissed without prejudice and with leave to amend as to the plaintiff's constitutional claims against other defendants; and (3) the court decline to exercise its supplemental jurisdiction over the plaintiff's causes of action arising under state law. name: D. Md. – Judge Julie R. Rubin
summary: In Charles G. Menk, III v. The Mitre Corp., No. 1:23-cv-00053-JRR (D. Md. Dec. 19, 2025), the court addressed a hallucinated citation included in the plaintiffs’ opposition to a motion to sever. The plaintiffs’ counsel explained that he used ChatGPT for preliminary research, which supplied the nonexistent citation; he provided those materials to co-counsel who drafted the filing, reviewed the response without cite-checking, signed it, accepted responsibility, apologized, and stated he would refrain from using ChatGPT for future legal issues. Citing Rule 11’s reasonable-inquiry requirement and Fourth Circuit guidance on sua sponte sanctions, the court declined to issue a Rule 11 show cause order in light of counsel’s transparency, contrition, and credibility, noting that the public docket entry sufficed as deterrence. The court warned, however, that any future citation to hallucinated authorities or similar conduct will prompt an order to show cause and potential Rule 11 sanctions and/or attorney-misconduct referral, and emphasized that if AI is used, “thorough verification of cited authorities is essential” to avoid rule violations and unnecessary consumption of court resources.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

P. 11 and can be sanctioned for “failing to conduct a ‘reasonable inquiry’ into whether ‘the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted by existing law.’” The court denied the plaintiff’s motion on other grounds.

name: N.D. Miss. – Judge Sharion Aycock
judge: Judge Sharion Aycock | Judge Sharion Marie Aycock
summary: In Disability Rts. Miss. v. Palmer Home for Children, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 263114 (N.D. Miss. Dec. 19, 2025), the plaintiff included various hallucinated citations in three separate motions. In response to the court’s order to show cause, the filing attorney stated that she “relied on an internal reference document developed for efficiency in drafting” and that the “citation errors” were due to “old-fashioned copy and paste” and “paraphrased summary lines for internal use only” that were not removed. The attorney also denied using any GenAI tools but admitted to failing to review certain cases pre-filing. Judge Aycock noted that this is the first instance that a Mississippi federal court considered an attorney’s misconduct with respect to citation mistakes (as opposed to those from a pro se litigant) and was “highly suspicious” that AI was used to generate the citations and did not believe the attorney’s explanations (because, for example, the purported the “summaries” the attorney drafted “misrepresent[ed], either entirely or in part, the facts and rulings of the cases cited”). However, because the attorney did not confirm her use of AI, the court did not conclude that GenAI was the cause of the errors, but noted that it “clearly demonstrate[d] an extreme deviation from [the attorney’s] professional and legal responsibilities.” The court found the attorney to have violated Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and acted in bad faith by “attempt[ing] to perpetrate fraud on the Court by citing fabricated legal authority in her filings and subsequently making certain misrepresentations.” As the review following the hallucinations was “a complete waste of valuable judicial resources,” Judge Aycock used her inherent powers to impose the following as sanctions: (i) ordering the Clerk of Court to send a copy of this decision to all district and magistrate judges in the district and the State Bar of Mississippi; (ii) ordering the Clerk of Court to file a copy of this decision in the other Northern District of Mississippi case where the plaintiff’s counsel is counsel of record; (iii) requiring plaintiff’s counsel to attend a 3-hour CLE class on AI hallucinations (separate from any CLE obligation under the Mississippi Bar) and submit a copy of her attendance; and (iv) requiring plaintiff’s counsel to pay the defendants $20,883.10 in attorney’s fees and costs within 30 days. The court specifically noted that the plaintiff, a “federally funded nonprofit agency,” was not responsible for the attorney’s misconduct, and further noted that the agency had retained new counsel and “accepted [the offending attorney’s] resignation.”
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: W.D. Va. – Judge Jasmine H. Yoon
summary: In Simpson v. Portfolio Recovery Assocs., LLC, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 262777 (W.D. Va. Dec. 19, 2025), the pro se plaintiff included various misrepresented and hallucinated citations in his motion for summary judgment. Although the court was sympathetic to the plaintiff’s “hurdles,” Judge Yoon noted that including false citations wastes resources and could constitute a violation of Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Judge Yoon warned the plaintiff that continuing to include hallucinated or inaccurate citations in future filings could result in an order to show cause as to why sanctions under Rule 11 would not be warranted.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

App. 3rd, Dec. 18, 2025), the pro se appellant’s brief contained citations to legal authority that were “at best incorrect, at worse fabricated.” The court ruled that regardless of whether the errors were the result of GenAI, it need not address arguments unsupported by legitimate legal authority. It declined to impose sanctions and affirmed the judgment below.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D.D.C. – Judge Beryl A. Howell
summary: In Zhang v. National Public Radio, Inc., No. 25-699 (BAH) (D.D.C. Dec. 18, 2025), the court sanctioned plaintiff’s counsel after striking an opposition brief that contained “two completely fictitious and eight seriously mischaracterized citations.” The court recounted counsel’s explanation that he relied on “summaries” from web searches that he was “not even aware” were “being generated by artificial intelligence,” and “failed to read at least 10 cases” cited in the brief. Concluding that the submission “unreasonably” multiplied proceedings and was “singularly egregious,” the court imposed sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927, directing counsel to reimburse the defendant for reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs associated with the stricken filing and the response to the court’s Order to Show Cause. The court also granted the defendant’s motion to dismiss the complaint in full.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Wis. – Chief Judge Pamela Pepper
summary: In Gerou v. George, No. 25-cv-1160-pp, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 261544 (E.D. Wis. Dec. 18, 2025), in an order addressing various motions, the court indicated its suspicion that the pro se petitioners cited GenAI hallucinated cases in their petition demanding proof of origination of funds. The petition contained “multiple direct quotes that do not appear in the cited cases” and citations to “multiple cases that the court could not locate in any legal database.” The court notes that neither “[c]arelessness, good faith, or ignorance,” nor petitioners’ “self-represented status,” excuse them from their obligation under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 to make a “reasonable inquiry into the supporting law.” Judge Pepper warned petitioners that they may be subject to monetary sanctions if they “file any more documents in any case in this district that contain citations to nonexistent cases or directly quote language that does not appear in a cited case.” The court dismissed the case on other grounds.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: Vt. Super. – Judge Benjamin D. Battles
summary: In Lafayette v. Abrami, 2025 Vt. Super. LEXIS 774 (Vt. Super. Dec. 18, 2025), the court imposed sanctions on the pro se plaintiff for his “repeated use of fake case citations and quotations” in multiple filings, including the initial complaint and preliminary injunction motion. The court further noted that the plaintiff had been warned by at least one other court regarding his use of fake citations. The plaintiff continued to file documents including fabricated cases and quotations after Judge Battles warned that he was considering sanctions. The court found that the plaintiff’s failure to confirm the validity of the cases on which he relied violated V.C.R.P. 11(b)(2). Considering the plaintiff’s history of “serial filings” which violate procedural rules, the plaintiff’s demonstrated bad faith, the burden imposed on the defendant, and the fact that no other sanction would be adequate, the court enjoined the plaintiff from filing any document in the Lamoille Civil Division pro se, unless the plaintiff first obtains permission from the judge.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Div. 4 – Judge Tamzarian, with Acting P.J. Collins and J. Mori concurring
summary: In Outreach v. Medoff, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 8133 (Cal. Ct. App. Dec. 17, 2025), the court struck appellant’s reply brief and sanctioned counsel after finding that “the majority of the case citations in the brief were incorrect in some significant way,” emphasizing that attorneys must read cited authorities to ensure they support the stated propositions and noting this duty applies to all court filings, not just appellate briefs. Counsel admitted the reply brief was filed “without [her] review” and that citations “are not correctly used or summarized”; the court rejected her new, inconsistent claim at oral argument that a paralegal filed the wrong version. Citing prior case precedent, the court underscored that filing briefs replete with fabricated or misused authorities—often associated with GenAI misuse—reflects a “‘fundamental abdicat[ion]’” of counsel’s responsibilities. The court imposed $5,070 in monetary sanctions payable to opposing counsel, ordered the opinion forwarded to the State Bar under Bus. & Prof. Code § 6086.7(a)(3), and required counsel to provide the opinion to her client and certify compliance; the underlying judgment was affirmed.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Ariz. – Judge Stephen M. McNamee
summary: In Dodge v. FirstService Residential Ariz. LLC, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 270557 (D. Ariz. Dec. 17, 2025), the plaintiff’s response to the defendant’s motion to dismiss contained “two misrepresented case holdings, five misquoted cases, and one case citation that does not exist.” During the hearing on the court’s order to show cause, plaintiff’s counsel admitted to using Federally Lawyer, an “add-on” to ChatGPT Enterprise that he uses “as a research and drafting tool to assist with his case load.” Given the delay in filing, plaintiff’s counsel stated that he did not independently verify the citations in the response brief and instead asked ChatGPT to perform a cite check using a prompt asking it to confirm that “all legal authority and citation[s] [are] up to date and accurate, meaning is it still good precedent, and are they all real cases?” Judge McNamee ultimately did not impose additional sanctions on the plaintiff’s attorney, the attorney self-reported his conduct to the State Bar of Arizona, and is manually reviewing filings in his other cases to report other errors. The court acknowledged the attorney’s caseload as a solo practitioner and found that the errors ultimately did not prejudice the plaintiff due to merits deficiencies. As such, the “public humiliation in this matter [was] a sufficient remedy.”
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Cal. – Magistrate Judge Dennis M. Cota
summary: In Lowe v. Vilsack, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 261126 (E.D. Cal. Dec. 17, 2025), the court denied Plaintiff’s Rule 30(d)(2) motion for sanctions arising from defense counsel’s conduct during the deposition of the defendant’s National Pandemic Coordinator. In so doing, the court chose to consider the plaintiff’s deposition record that was allegedly created using an AI tool called “Readback Active Reporting” over the defendant’s objection that the process violated Fed. R. Civ. P. 28 and 30. A representative from Readback joined the deposition for its entirety. The defendant described the Readback AI tool as “court reporting reimagined—a remote reporting service powered by patented AI technology and human editors that delivers transcripts at breakneck speeds.” In response, the plaintiff provided evidence from Readback that the company does not use AI “to generate the transcript.” The court concluded that the deposition transcript bore sufficient “indicia of reliability” for the court to consider it for purposes of the sanctions motion, despite any allegation of GenAI use. The court admonished both sides and threatened sanctions for reasons unrelated to GenAI use.

name: N.D. Ill.  – Judge Iain D. Johnston

Taking into account the posture of the case and the plaintiff's pro se status, Judge Johnston did not impose sanctions, but “admonish[ed the plaintiff] . . .  that quotations attributed to cases should only come directly from those cases.” The court denied the plaintiff's motion to remand and dismissed the complaint on other grounds without prejudice to the plaintiff filing an amended complaint.

summary: In in re Bryant, 2025 Bankr. LEXIS 3390 (Bankr. M.D.N.C. At the hearing, the court declined to issue sanctions, instead reminding the debtors of their obligations to the court under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9011, which requires unrepresented parties to not make inaccurate or improper filings to the court. When the debtors continued to make arguments that were “frivolous” and unsupported by existing law, including arguments that had previously been rejected by the court, Judge Kahn reminded the debtors that, “fictitious cases and cites are not the only way litigants present frivolous arguments.” Judge Kahn cautioned that “further violations of Rule 9011 will result in sanctions that will include striking pleadings, denying relief requested, and monetary sanctions.” On unrelated grounds, the court denied the debtors’ motion against defendants for sanctions for violating automatic stay and discharge injunction.

name: D. Conn. – Judge Vernon D. Oliver
summary: In Braica v. Frankowski, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 263098 (D. Conn. Dec. 15, 2025), the pro se plaintiff included various unrelated and hallucinated citations in his brief in response to the defendant’s partial motion to dismiss, which the court found to be “highly indicative of unvetted AI use.” The plaintiff attempted to rectify these errors by filing a sur-reply without seeking the court’s leave but maintained that some of his unrelated cases were applicable and continued to cite to hallucinated and irrelevant cases. In response to the court’s order to show cause, the plaintiff admitted to using “publicly available websites” but did not admit to using any GenAI tool. Judge Oliver found the plaintiff’s failure to verify and correct his citations and the fact that he “minimized the role of AI in his filings” to be violative of Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Given the “interests of justice and deterrence,” the court struck both the response and sur-reply without leave to amend and warned the plaintiff that “more stringent Rule 11 sanctions” could be imposed if he submits another filing with GenAI hallucinations.

name: D. Kan. – Judge Julie A. Robinson
summary: In Lexos Media IP, LLC v. Overstock.com, Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 258649 (D. Kan. Dec. 15, 2025), the court granted in part and denied in part the plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a corrected opposition to a Daubert motion after the defendant identified “nonexistent quotations,” “nonexistent or incorrect citations,” and “misrepresentations about cited authority” in the plaintiff’s original brief—errors the plaintiff attributed to counsel’s unverified use of GenAI. The court held that allowing substantive changes would function as an improper sur-reply and that Plaintiff failed to show excusable neglect under Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b), emphasizing the prejudice to the defendant and the waste of judicial resources caused by the defective filing. Citing recent authority warning that careless use of GenAI can waste resources and undermine credibility, the court declined to permit a “do-over,” denied any additions of text or authority, and struck the original response. The court ordered Plaintiff to file by December 19, 2025, a corrected brief that omits all nonexistent quotations, nonexistent/incorrect/inapposite citations, and misrepresentations about cited authority, noting that sanctions would be addressed separately.

R. Civ. P. 11’s requirement that parties’ arguments are “warranted by existing law.” Judge Dorsey warned that additional reliance on “inaccurate or fake authority” may result in sanctions. name: D.N.J. – Judge Leo. M. Gordon
summary: In Gardner v. Combs, No. 2:24-cv-07729, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 258523 (D.N.J. Dec. 15, 2025), the plaintiff’s counsel cited to a nonexistent case and “fabricated legal propositions derived from [GenAI] in support of Plaintiff's opposition to Defendants’ motions to dismiss.” Counsel failed to provide an explanation for the false citation after oral argument despite numerous inquiries by defendant’s counsel, leading the court to issue an order to show cause. In response to the order to show cause, counsel admitted that the error was the result of GenAI and “took ‘full responsibility’” for the mistake. The attorney had previously been sanctioned for GenAI use in another jurisdiction, and Judge Gordon noted that despite him taking preventative “corrective actions,” counsel “nevertheless again failed to act with diligence and address issues arising from his reliance on AI research.” The court concluded that his “negligent reliance on unverified (AI-hallucinated) case law and subsequent failure to communicate with respect to the court's follow-up inquiry” violated Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. The court imposed a $6,000 sanction on the attorney, describing the penalty as “on the higher end of the range due to his repeated behavior. The court also ordered that counsel self-report the opinion and order to show cause to NJ and NY attorney licensing entities and serve copies on “his client and discuss their implications with her.”

name: D.N.M. – Magistrate Judge Steven C. Yarbrough
summary: In Maturin v. T-Mobile USA, Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 258578 (D.N.M. Dec. 15, 2025), the court recommended granting in part and denying in part defendant’s motion for sanctions alleging bad-faith conduct and frivolous pleadings, ordering the plaintiff to pay defendant’s reasonable expenses for investigating “false citations” used in the plaintiff’s filings and for litigating the sanctions motion and supplement. The court further recommended that, in all future filings, the plaintiff must disclose any use of AI in drafting and certify under Rule 11 that all AI-provided information, including all case citations, has been verified for accuracy. While denying terminating sanctions, the court warned that failure to comply with court orders or sanctions may result in dismissal, and permitted defendant to seek additional sanctions for noncompliance.

name: D.S.C. – Magistrate Judge William S. Brown
summary: In Jeter v. Adusa Transp. LLC, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 270555 (D.S.C. December 15, 2025), the pro se plaintiff’s response to defendant’s motion to dismiss cited nonexistent authorities, misquoted existing case law, and invoked cases for propositions they do not support—conduct the court observed is “consistent with on the use of [GenAI] . . . . without proper verification.” The court cautioned that misusing GenAI in this manner “may violate Rule 11” and emphasized that misquotations and nonexistent authorities reflect failing to read governing law. Given the novelty of GenAI and the plaintiff’s pro se status, the court declined sanctions but instructed that any GenAI-assisted submissions must be verified by reading the actual cases, rules, and statutes. The court warned that continued failure to verify citations and quotations will wrongfully multiply proceedings and may evidence bad faith, exposing the plaintiff to sanctions in the future. The court recommended granting in part and denying in part the motion to dismiss on other grounds.

name: M.D. Pa. – Judge Julia K. Munley
summary: In Williams v. Assistant DA John R. Canavan, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 258853 (M.D. Pa. Dec. 15, 2025), the court addressed the pro se plaintiff’s reliance on GenAI in multiple filings, noting an “uptick” in pro se litigants using “cut-and-paste AI outputs” and finding that the plaintiff’s guardian-ad-litem motion included an AI “hallucination.” The court also observed AI-aided objections that included a table of authorities mismatched to the filing and stylistic discrepancies from Plaintiff’s handwritten IFP motion. Citing Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2)-(c), the court warned the plaintiff that future “unchecked reliance on AI . . . will result in sanctions,” including striking pleadings and dismissal with prejudice. Substantively, the court dismissed the pro se plaintiff’s claims without prejudice on other grounds.

name: C.D. Cal. – Judge Fred W. Slaughter
summary: In N.Z. v. Fenix Int’l Ltd., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 259988 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 12, 2025), the court denied the plaintiffs’ motion for leave to withdraw multiple opposition briefs and file “corrective” briefs after identifying AI-generated inaccuracies, and imposed Rule 11 sanctions on the plaintiff’s counsel and co-counsel for misuse of GenAI and failure to verify AI-modified content. The court found that four opposition briefs contained hallucinated authorities, mischaracterized law and quotations, and incorrect record citations—including misstatements of the court’s prior order—and held that allowing corrective briefs would “not remediate, but rather exacerbate” prejudice where defendants had already expended substantial resources addressing the tainted filings and where proposed corrections still contained errors. The plaintiff’s counsel also admitted to using ChatGPT to “draft large portions of the briefs, analyze the legal research [the attorney] performed,” and “combine and shorten” materials. The court also observed that the attorney failed to realize when ChatGPT modified text and authorities, did not verify accuracy, and did not inform her co-counsel of her GenAI use; and co-counsel, relying on the drafting attorney’s prior work and facing a deadline, did not perform a full cite check. Concluding that counsel had certified content not warranted by existing law and failed to supervise consistent with Cal. R. Prof’l Conduct 5.1 and the court’s AI standing order, the court sanctioned both the primary offending individual attorney and his law firm (jointly and severally) $10,000 and sanctioned the plaintiffs’ individual co-counsel $3,000, required status reporting on remedial measures and certification that all future citations accurately support the asserted propositions, directed service of the order on the California and Arizona state bars and each individual plaintiff, and discharged the order to show cause.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Or. – Magistrate Judge Mark D. Clarke
summary: In Couvrette v. Wisnovsky, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 273533 (D. Or. Dec. 12, 2025), the court imposed sanctions on the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs’ attorney for filing three briefs containing fabricated cases and quotations, which the court held constituted violations of Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and local rules. The plaintiffs continued to cite to nonexistent cases after the defendants called the errors to their attention and suggested GenAI misuse. In response to the defendants’ motion for sanctions, the plaintiffs simply deleted the non-existent citations and quotation marks while leaving the fabricated legal contentions unchanged. Plaintiffs argued that “[t]he inclusion of inaccurate citations was inadvertent and the result of reliance on an automated legal citation tool” and that they had taken proper corrective action. Defendants then re-filed their motion for sanctions. At the sanctions hearing, the court found that the plaintiffs failed to take corrective action and instead “attempted a coverup,” violating Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and the Oregon Rules of Professional Conduct. The court also found the plaintiff himself was likely the person using GenAI to draft and “share[d] responsibility [with his counsel] for the use of non-existent cases and fabricated quotations,” thus warranting sanctions against the plaintiff as well. As sanction, the court struck without leave to refile plaintiffs’ summary judgment briefing; imposed a $15,500 fine plus attorney’s fees and expenses on the plaintiff’s counsel; vacated the order allowing former local counsel to withdraw and ordered him show cause why he should not be subject to sanctions; and dismissed the plaintiff’s claims with prejudice.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: S.D.N.Y. – Magistrate Judge Gary Stein
summary: In Matthew NG v. Amguard Ins. Co., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 260114 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 12, 2025), the court noted an inaccurate citation in the plaintiff’s letter motion that “provides no support” for the proposition asserted and assumed the filing “may have been drafted with the assistance of a [GenAI] tool.” The court expressly directed compliance with Judge Broderick’s Individual Rule 4(J) (which requires any party who uses GenAI in preparing a filing to disclose that use and to certify independent review and accuracy verification of all AI-drafted portions). While denying the plaintiff’s requests on service and a stay, the court set a deadline for the plaintiff to file either an opposition to the motion to dismiss or an amended complaint and emphasized future adherence to the court’s AI disclosure and verification rule.

name: N.C. Super. Ct. – Senior Resident Superior Court Judge Martin B. McGee
judge: Senior Resident Superior Court Judge Martin B. McGee
summary: Judge McGee’s Revised Administrative Order on Artificial Intelligence for Judicial District 25 supersedes the court’s prior July 23, 2024 order, applies immediately to all civil and criminal proceedings in Cabarrus County, and lays out requirements for AI use and disclosure, concerning both court filings and evidentiary issues.  While the order does not bar the use of GenAI for litigation purposes, it reminds litigants that each submission to the court is the ultimate responsibility of the signing attorney or party, and requires  "[h]uman-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight” (i.e, having a human decision-maker “independently review, verify, and approve any AI output before it is relied on, acted on, or submitted in any court proceeding”). The order also reminds attorneys of their professional duties to “maintain technical competence regarding” the technologies used and to ensure they do not place confidential or privileged information into public AI tools. With respect to recording and transcription, the order provides that only official reporters or clerks may use AI tools to capture, record, transcribe, process, or alter audio or video without judicial authorization. Jurors are prohibited from using GenAI for any purpose, while litigants may use GenAI for non-disruptive legal research during hearings with appropriate attorney oversight. Finally, the order requires that parties must disclose no later than 90 days before trial if they have used GenAI to “generate[], offer[], materially alter[], enhance[] or analyze[]” evidence. After that window, disclosure must be immediate. By contrast, non-substantive AI use (such as “word processing, spell-check, grammar or “administrative tasks,” GenAI use in discovery, and use of GenAI to aid court reporters or transcriptionists) does not require disclosure. When there is reasonable basis for doubt as to the accuracy of a document, parties must use “best efforts” to verify the evidence’s validity and must meet and confer to resolve concerns about AI-generated evidence (and such concerns must be raised before trial absent extraordinary circumstances). Should parties fail to comply with this order, the court may impose sanctions, but the court will favorably consider “timely, good-faith disclosures” and taking “reasonable steps to verify authenticity and reliability.”
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: Pa. Sup. Ct. Interim Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence – Judicial Officers and Court Personnel
summary: Effective December 8, 2025, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s Interim Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers and Court Personnel governs court personnel’s use of GenAI tools and provides insight for parties on how to approach the use of GenAI. The policies define GenAI as an all-encompassing term for “algorithms and/or computer processes that use artificial intelligence to generate text, audio, or images based on user prompts.” Before any GenAI tool is used, it must first be approved by court leadership who ensure that the tool will keep information “confidential and privileged.” Court personnel must, however, presume that GenAI inputs will not be treated as confidential and privileged and remain aware of GenAI’s “capabilities and limitations,” including hallucinations, biases, and inaccuracies. The court welcomes GenAI use by its personnel for, among other things, document summaries, preliminary legal research, and drafts and edits of their own work. Ultimately, the GenAI user remains responsible for the output’s completeness and accuracy.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Research

name: W.D. Pa. – Judge Marilyn J. Horan
summary: In Mullins v. Duquesne Univ. of the Holy Spirit, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 251137 (W.D. Pa. Dec. 5, 2025), the court granted the defendant’s motion to strike the pro se plaintiff’s reply brief where the plaintiff misused of GenAI by including multiple citation and quotation errors “that appear to be the result of Plaintiff using [GenAI] drafting tools,” including a “phantom quote.” The plaintiff “implict[ly]” admitted to using GenAI tools, which resulted in hallucinations, but the court criticized his “unwillingness to affirmatively admit” to such use. Emphasizing that neither the court nor opposing counsel is responsible for “fact‑checking” a party’s filings, the court held that filing AI‑generated content without thorough pre‑filing verification “wastes” judicial and party resources. The court therefore: (1) struck the reply but granted leave to refile a corrected version; and (2) ordered that all future filings must include a certification disclosing whether “he has utilized any [AI] drafting tools in the research and/or drafting of the document being filed,” identifying each AI tool, pinpointing the specific AI‑generated portions, and certifying the accuracy of all citations and authorities, warning that violations may trigger sanctions under Rule 11 or other authority.

name: Cal. Super. –  Judge Michael B. Wilson
summary: In Gibbs v. City of Compton, 2025 Cal. Super. LEXIS 73275 (Cal. Super. Dec. 4, 2025), the court found the plaintiff's opposition to the defendant’s motion to set aside default judgment “unreliable” on its face and that the plaintiff’s counsel drafted it using GenAI without properly reviewing it for accuracy. The court reached these conclusions because the plaintiff's filings (including a declaration by the plaintiff’s counsel) incorrectly asserted that defendant's memorandum violated the page limit, misquoted a court form, and included a nonexistent case quotation. The court also found GenAI output language at the end of the plaintiff’s opposition briefing that clearly demonstrated that “Plaintiff’s counsel utilized an AI tool to draft and submit the papers.” Judge Wilson therefore “disregard[ed] improper citations and arguments lacking proper legal citation” and “exercise[d] [the court’s] discretion to afford the declaration accompanying Plaintiff's Opposition less credence,” declining to consider the plaintiff’s arguments because of lack of legal support. The court ultimately granted the defendant’s motion to set aside the entry of default and default judgment.

name: N.D. Ill. – Judge Rebecca R. Pallmeyer
summary: In Dorsey v. Ponce, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 250368 (N.D. Ill. Dec. 4, 2025), the court expressed concerns about generative AI-fabricated citations in the pro se plaintiff’s briefing. name: W.D. Okla. – Chief Judge Timothy D. DeGiusti
summary: In Hill v. Okla. Cnty. Crim. Just. Auth., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 250359 (W.D. Okla. The court required plaintiff’s counsel to pay attorney’s fees and costs associated with the show-cause hearing; disclose in all future pleadings whether GenAI was used, identify the specific tool was used, and certify that any AI‑drafted portions (including all citations and legal authorities) have been checked for accuracy; and complete (within 90 days) at least three hours of CLE in ethics or legal technology, including at least one hour on the use of GenAI in the legal context.

name: 10th Cir. – Judges Timothy M. Tymkovich, Bobby R. Baldock, Gregory A. Phillips

summary: In Moore v. City of Del. City, 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 31411 (10th Cir. Dec. 3, 2025), the court dismissed the pro se appellant’s case for citing eleven nonexistent cases and misrepresenting the holdings of at least two cases in her opening brief. R. App. P. 28(a)(8)(A)’s requirement that an appellant's brief cite supporting authority.” The court dismissed the appeal and ordered that the appellant disclose GenAI use and verify the accuracy of her citations in future filings. Finally, the court warned “future litigants, pro se and those represented by counsel alike, that outright dismissal—without a merits ruling—may be an appropriate sanction in a given case,” as may monetary or other sanctions (including awarding the opposing party’s attorney fees incurred from the “unscrutinized use of GenAI”).

summary: In United States v. Boehm, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 235285, the pro se defendant included inaccurate legal arguments and quotations “that appear to be generated by [GenAI] using legitimate case citations” in his request for an order clarifying the conditions of his supervised release. summary: In Charles Ringo v. Colquhoun Design Studio, LLC, 2025 Ore. App. LEXIS 1957 (Or. Ct. App. Dec. 3, 2025), the court directed respondents’ counsel to pay $2,000 for submitting a brief “littered with fabricated cases, a fabricated quotation, and fabricated substantive law.” Judge Ashby noted that the fabricated cases “likely” resulted from GenAI use and constitute a violation of ORCP 17C(3)’s certification that “the claims, defenses, and other legal positions taken in the pleading, motion or other document are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for the extension, modification or reversal of existing law or the establishment of new law,” as well as a violation of the attorney’s professional duties. The court described how the attorney’s conduct “strain[ed] [the court’s] limited judicial resources” and “jeopardizes the rule of law,” as “[t]he injection of false precedent into the practice of law shakes the foundation of our judicial system.” Judge Ashby thus ordered monetary sanctions of $500 for each false citation and $1,000 for each false quotation or statement of law, totaling to $2,000. The court allowed counsel to resubmit the stricken brief, but required that all submissions by this counsel going forward “contain a certification that (1) counsel drafted the brief and did not use [GenAI] to produce a draft of the brief; (2) counsel has read each case and each other source of law cited in the brief; and (3) counsel has verified that every source of law cited, quoted[,] or paraphrased exists.”

summary: In Magee v. New Balance Athletics., Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 234410 (E.D. Ark. name: E.D. Mich. –  Judge F. Kay Behm
summary: In Jarrus v. Governor of Michigan, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 234830, the pro se plaintiffs objected to the Magistrate Judge’s order for the plaintiffs to show cause for the use of GenAI in drafting their motion to amend their complaint. Judge Behm suspected that the plaintiffs again used GenAI in their objection. The court noted that the plaintiffs’ briefing appeared to be “nothing more than a copy-paste from a chatbot-style generative AI tool” with a “series of . . . false citations” of real cases with explanations that did not match the real case. Judge Behm noted that the use of GenAI for drafting without independent citation checking “unquestionably” violates Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. After the Magistrate Judge's warning (see Jarrus v. Governor of Michigan, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 221984 (E.D. Mich. Nov. 7, 2025)), the court ordered plaintiffs to show cause why they should not be sanctioned. Judge Behm highlighted that Rule 11 “imposes obligations on each and every signatory to a briefing, not just the person who was the primary drafter.” Thus, even though one of the plaintiffs did not draft the documents and only reviewed them at a “very general level” before signing, the court held her “equally responsible for the use of misrepresented or otherwise improper citations,” and warned that further misconduct could result in “a dismissal of her claims in their entirety.” Although the plaintiffs admitted to misusing GenAI (ChatGPT specifically) in their filings, the court found that sanctions were warranted. Judge Behmt adopted Magistrate Judge Patti's recommendation of $200 per GenAI citation and imposed a $600 fine ($300 per plaintiff), warning that failure to pay may result in dismissal. The court reasoned that one of the plaintiff's $20 per month spending on a ChatGPT subscription suggested an ability to pay sanctions. The court further warned that it will consider dismissal of the case if the plaintiffs file further briefings “with even a single misrepresented, misquoted, or fictitious case that is caused by the use of [GenAI].”

name: Cal. Ct. App. – Judge William F. Fahey
summary: In Shayan v. Shakib, 2025 LEXIS 595242 (Cal. Ct. App. 2d. Dec. 1, 2025), the appellant's attorney filed a brief containing numerous fabricated case citations and a transcript from a hearing in a different matter, and the respondent asked the court to strike the brief and dismiss the appeal as a sanction. In response, the appellant’s attorney claimed that the errors were the result of his staff failing to replace placeholder language from the draft brief, not the result of GenAI use, that he checked each citation, and that the errors reflected only “minor” wording differences. The court disagreed with that the attorney’s characterization and noted that both the brief and the opposition contained “inaccurate representations of case holdings.” The court held that these errors violated local rules, the Ca. Code Civ. Proc., and the rules of professional conduct, regardless of whether the fabrications were the result of GenAI use. Furthermore, Judge Fahey observed that even if the attorney did review the accuracy of the citations, “the rules of this court require him to present accurate, truthful representations of the facts and law to this court,” which the attorney “did not do.” The court ordered that the attorney pay $7,500 in sanctions to the clerk of court (due to the time the court spent verifying the citations, the attorney's failure to accept responsibility, and the continued mistakes in the opposition motion) and also struck the appellant’s opening brief and required the filing of a corrected brief within 10 days. Judge Fahey served a copy of the order on the State Bar.

name: D. Colo. – Magistrate Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell
summary: In her guidance document entitled “Guidance on Responsible AI Use in Court Proceedings,” Magistrate Judge Braswell provides a framework for parties practicing before her court to address AI-related issues, particularly hallucinations in court filings. Notably, the guidance “is not an order and does not establish new rules or requirements” and “should [not] be interpreted to modify or supersede any applicable law, rule, professional obligation, or order issued by another judge.” The guidance acknowledges that AI “presents opportunities for innovation, growth, and increased access to justice” and encourages parties to “learn to leverage it responsibly,” while also noting the various “challenge[s]” that AI poses, only “one part” of which is hallucinations. The court’s guidance emphasizes that “all inaccurate statements made to a tribunal, regardless of how they were generated, are a serious matter,” and that the “same rules apply” regardless of the source of the error. When hallucinations are found, the guidance encourages parties to confer to explore remedial measures, inform the court, and escalate only if the drafter refuses to engage in good faith. The guidance lists a variety of factors the court will consider when evaluating submission of AI hallucinations, including whether the drafter engaged in good faith, took responsibility, took immediate steps to mitigate harm, follows an AI Use Policy, took reasonable steps to verify accuracy before filing, and whether the drafter is a pro se party.  The court will also consider the nature and extent of the hallucinations, whether they caused meaningful prejudice, and whether they resulted in a significant waste of judicial resources. Finally, the guidance encourages caution in the legal industry regarding AI-created bias, ensuring adequate data privacy safeguards, and ensuring human autonomy over important decisions.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Tex. – Chief Judge Amos L. Mazzant
summary: Effective December 1, 2025, Judge Mazzant’s General Order 25-07 (E.D. Tex. Oct. 31, 2025) amends the Eastern District of Texas Local Rule CV-11(g) on GenAI use. Prior to the amendment, the rule warned only pro se litigants that they “remain responsible for the accuracy and quality” of their submissions to the court and cautioned that GenAI “may produce factually or legally inaccurate content.” As revised, all litigants are now “bound by the requirements of Fed. R. Civ. P. 11” and must “review and verify all content” (rather than just “computer-generated content,” as the Rule previously required) when using GenAI. Judge Mazzant’s Comment indicated that the amendments were prompted by an “increasing number of filings” where litigants “fail[ed] to review and verify the factual and legal accuracy” of content produced by GenAI. The parallel rule for attorneys, Local Rule AT-3(m), was also amended to conform to LR CV-11(g).
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: M.D. Fla. – Judge William F. Jung
summary: In Bey v. Glass, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 233422 (M.D. Fla. Dec. 1, 2025), the pro se plaintiff cited a nonexistent case in his complaint. Judge Jung suspected that the hallucinated citation was the result of GenAI use in drafting after the court “cannot find . . . based on independent research” a case the plaintiff cited and warned the plaintiff that the court has the “inherent authority” under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 to impose sanctions for GenAI use, “including the complete dismissal and termination of the case.” The court dismissed the plaintiff's complaint without prejudice on other grounds.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: D. Colo. – Magistrate Judge Kathryn A. Starnella
summary: In Hanson v. Nest Home Lending, LLC, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 233214 (D. Colo. Nov. 28, 2025), the court made absolute its prior order to show cause after finding that the pro se plaintiffs’ complaint, motions, and responses contained “fabricated legal authority” and “hallucinated citations” in violation of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11. The plaintiffs argued they acted in good faith and that any errors stemmed from their “ignorance of the law,” but the court held that Rule 11’s objective‑reasonableness standard applies to all filers, including pro se litigants, and that good faith does not excuse submission of fake or inaccurate citations. The court emphasized the harms caused by such misuse, including wasted party and judicial resources, diversion from merits issues, and reputational harm to the legal system, and noted that plaintiffs had been on notice of problems in their complaint yet continued filing papers with fictitious or mischaracterized authority. The court further observed that plaintiffs’ response compounded the issue by misquoting precedent and citing out‑of‑jurisdiction law for irrelevant propositions. Magistrate Judge Starnella recommended sweeping non‑monetary remedies tailored to deterrence and docket integrity, including striking the tainted filings identified in the show‑cause order, granting the plaintiffs 45 days to file an amended complaint, and requiring that all future filings include a detailed certification, in table format, listing each citation, confirming its existence and that it supports the proposition asserted, and identifying the source where the authority was obtained. The court also directed plaintiffs to use “legitimate” research databases and to contact the Federal Pro Se Clinic regarding publicly available research resources. The court denied pending motions to dismiss as moot in light of its recommendation and warned that continued misconduct could lead to dismissal. While recognizing the increasing use of GenAI, the court underscored that parties must independently verify accuracy and that “using a fake opinion to support an argument is a violation of Rule 11(b)(2),” regardless of intent.

name: C.D. Cal. – Judge Stanley Blumenfeld, Jr.
summary: In Anaya v. Target Corp., No. 2:25-cv-09135-SB-RAO (Nov. 26, 2025), the court sanctioned plaintiff's counsel in the amount of $1,250 for filing a brief “containing a case that did not stand for the cited proposition” in support of the plaintiff's motion to remand. Judge Blumenfeld noted that the court had previously cautioned the plaintiff about the importance of abiding by court rules, warning that further violations could result in sanctions. In response to the order to show cause, the attorney explained that his associate used “AI to refine a small portion of the Reply" but he did not disclose the use because he did not realize the associate had used GenAI at the time. Judge Blumenfeld determined that this conduct violated Fed. R. Civ. P. 11. The court further “admonished” the firm's managing partner based on his “indirect responsibility” for “failing to take appropriate steps to ensure firmwide compliance with all applicable rules and orders.” Judge Blumenfeld determined that the despite his candor, the filing attorney’s “use of AI without proper disclosure and blatant misuse of case law in reliance on AI—coupled with his careless oversight of the case as lead counsel for Plaintiff—warrant appropriate sanctions.” The court ordered $1,250 in monetary sanctions and notification of the sanction to the State Bar of California.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: M.D. Fla. – Judge Sheri Polster Chappell
summary: In Doc App, Inc. v. Leafwell, Inc., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232188 (M.D. Fla. Nov. 26, 2025), the court granted the defendant’s motion for sanctions after the plaintiff’s counsel included various inaccurate citations (including to nonexistent and out-of-context cases) in its motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction. The court found that the plaintiff’s attorney violated Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b) for including erroneous citations due to his “reckless use of AI.” The court concluded that sanctions were particularly warranted where counsel responded to the court’s order to show cause in a “colossal [] collection of excuses and projection” with a “defiant tone and condescending communications with and about his opposing counsel,” and where plaintiff’s counsel was not forthcoming about his use of AI. Judge Chappell held that the attorney failed to take responsibility for his actions and reminded him of his role as “an officer of the court” with “a duty of candor to the tribunal.” As sanctions, Judge Chappell ordered plaintiff’s counsel to: (i) pay the defendant’s attorneys’ fees and costs associated with their response to the motion; (ii) file a copy of this order to any complaint filed in the next 2 years in the Middle District of Florida; (iii) attend a Florida CLE class on legal ethics and AI by January 30, 2026 and file a certificate of completion by February 20, 2026; and (iv) send a copy of this order to his client’s CEO and file an affidavit confirming that the CEO has read the order. The court also referred plaintiff’s counsel to the Florida Bar for “appropriate discipline” and asked the clerk to send the entire case record to the Florida Bar.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: S.D.N.Y. – Judge Vernon S. Broderick
summary: In Peak v. Maraj-Petty, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232924 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 26, 2025), in an order continuing the stay of the case, Judge Broderick raised his concern that the pro se plaintiff was using GenAI throughout the litigation “because of his persistent misquotes and interpretation of cases.” Most recently, the plaintiff included two hallucinated quotations in an opposition letter. Though the court was sympathetic to the plaintiff’s status of representation, the plaintiff was reminded of Individual Rule of Practice in Civil Cases 4(J) that requires parties to disclose any use of AI and certify that all GenAI-drafted portions are verified and accurate.

name: D. Conn. – Judge Vernon D. Oliver
summary: In Andre v. Warden, FCI Danbury, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232986 (D. Conn. Nov. 25, 2025), the pro se petitioner filed a motion for relief from judgment that, when considered in light of other pleadings, appeared “unusually well-written and formatted for a pro se litigant” and prompted the court to think they were drafted by an attorney. Upon further review, the court discovered that the motion contained “multiple significant hallucinations” and inaccurate citations. During the hearing on the court’s order to show cause, the petitioner admitted that he heavily relied on AI tools during the drafting process and even asked some of his “friends” to “ask AI certain questions” and then have “AI ‘draft up motions.’” Judge Oliver found that the petitioner acted in “subjective bad faith,” thereby violating Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, because he made “misrepresentations to the Court as to the origins of the filings” by directing “third parties to use generative AI and then concealed his actions from the Court when given the opportunity to accept responsibility.” As sanctions, the court ultimately struck the petitioner’s motion for relief with prejudice.

name: Ill. App. 2d Dist. – Judge Susan F. Hutchinson
summary: In Pletcher v. Vill. of Libertyville Police Pension Bd., No. 2-24-0416, 2025 Ill. App. Unpub. LEXIS 2115 (Nov. 24, 2025), the court granted defendant’s motion for sanctions against the pro se plaintiff pursuant to Illinois Supreme Court Rule 375(a). Specifically, the plaintiff filed a complaint for an administrative review of the Village of Libertyville Pension Board’s decision on plaintiff’s application for disability pension and a supporting brief. The court found that the plaintiff’s brief cited to multiple cases that do not exist, and also cited to “actual cases” but with “fictitious quotes and holdings.” The court concluded that these fictitious citations were “hallucinated by [GenAI]” and that the plaintiff violated Rule 341(h)(7). As a result, the court sanctioned the plaintiff by striking plaintiff’s brief and dismissing his appeal.

Nov. 21, 2025), the court suspected that the pro se plaintiffs “prepared certain filings with the assistance of a [GenAI] service.” The court warned the parties that any filings prepared using GenAI must include a declaration disclosing the GenAI use and certifying that the filer independently verified the accuracy of the contents as in compliance with Fed. name: Del. Ch. – Senior Magistrate Selena E. Molina
summary: In Gupta v. Safko et al., No. CV 2024-1296-SEM, 2025 WL 3269046, at *1 (Del. Ch. Nov. 21, 2025), the court denied defendants’ request that pro plaintiff should be sanctioned. Although the court concluded that the plaintiff’s filings “do appear to have been generated through GenAI,” because of his pro se status and the fact that there was no “clear showing” of hallucinations or “glaring” misrepresentations, the court ultimately declined to impose sanctions. Senior Magistrate Molina did, however, order that the plaintiff must not only “ensure every future filing” is accurate, but also “certify any future use of GenAI” to the court by identifying what GenAI tool was used and how, and that it was reviewed for accuracy.

name: Del. Ch. Ct. – Senior Magistrate Judge Selena E. Molina
judge: Senior Magistrate Judge Selena E. Molina
summary: In Anuj Gupta v. Safko, 2025 Del. Ch. LEXIS 2041 (Del. Ch. Nov. 21, 2025), the defendants requested sanctions under Court of Chancery Rule 11, as the pro se plaintiff seemingly generated his filings with a GenAI tool. Judge Molina indicated that this conduct “raises several concerns about the Plaintiff’s ability to satisfy Rule 11’s dictates,” wastes parties’ and the court’s resources, and poses “reputational harms to the legal system.” However, given the plaintiff’s pro se status and lack of “any clear showing of hallucinations or glaring legal or factual misrepresentations in his filings,” the court declined to impose sanctions. Nevertheless, the court did order the plaintiff to certify any future use of GenAI and warned that “this leniency will not continue” should the plaintiff fail to comply with the court’s certification requirement.

name: Minn. Dist. – Judge Laurie J. Miller
summary: In Nuvola, LLC v. Wright, 2025 Minn. Dist. LEXIS 5940 (Minn. Dist. Nov. 21, 2025), the defendant’s counsel “cited multiple non-existent cases” in his motion to compel arbitration. The court set a hearing for the defendant’s attorney to explain the non-existent caselaw, and for the plaintiff’s counsel to explain why he did not bring the issue to the court’s attention. In response, the defendant’s counsel apologized to the court for submitting non-existent citations, and admitted to using GenAI but claimed that he expected the program to generate a brief only using the verified cases he had provided it. Judge Miller concluded that the attorney’s conduct violated Minn. R. Civ. P. 11.02(b)’s requirement that an attorney certifies, in presenting a document to the court, that “the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions there are warranted by existing law,” and Minn. Stat. § 549.211’s requirement that pleadings are grounded in law. As sanction, the court referred the defendant’s attorney to the Minnesota Lawyers Professional Responsibility Board; directed him to “conduct five (5) presentations to lawyers and/or law students on the dangers of using artificial intelligence in the legal profession”; and imposed a financial penalty of $1,000. The court also noted that the plaintiff’s counsel “offered little explanation for his failure to check the citations in Defendant’s brief.” While the court did not sanction the plaintiff’s attorney, Judge Miller “remind[ed] counsel that it is the obligation of counsel on both sides to respond to each other's arguments, including completing a basic cite-check of the cases cited by the other side.”

name: S.D. Fla. – Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz II
summary: In Dubinin v. Papazian, No. 25-CV-23877-RAR, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 229362 (S.D. Fla. Nov. 21, 2025), following the court’s orders to show cause why plaintiff’s counsel should not be sanctioned for “cites to non-existent cases and quotations in a brief that appeared to be drafted using [GenAI],” plaintiff’s attorney denied using AI, but “admitted to filing a brief riddled with inaccuracies,” claiming the drafting had been delegated to another attorney. The court reviewed the two attorneys’ other filings in different matters and found that the two attorneys had previously been caught submitting filings that “may have been drafted using [GenAI].” Because of the filing attorney’s “misconduct in this case and others, including her misrepresentations to the Court,” and the fact that her “use of AI was ‘so egregious that this Court finds that [it was] done in bad faith,’” the court concluded that sanctions are appropriate under the court’s inherent powers, Local Rule 6(b)(2)(A) of the Southern District of Florida, and 28 U.S.C. § 1927. The court ultimately struck plaintiff’s complaint and dismissed the action without prejudice, ordered the filing attorney to pay defendant’s attorney fees, and referred both the filing and drafting attorneys to the Florida Bar and Grievance Committee.

summary: In Clayman v. Bessant, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232878 (S.D. Fla. Nov. 21, 2025), the pro se plaintiff admitted that the only cited case in his motion to alter or amend an order was an “AI-generated hallucination.” The court noted that the plaintiff is permitted to use AI for drafting assistance but must ensure that all cases are accurate. Judge Matthewman also provided a “final warning” that the plaintiff could face sanctions and a restricted filing if he continues to misuse AI. name: Supreme Court of N.Y.S., Richmond County – Judge Wayne M. Ozzi
summary: In Grymes Dev. Co. v. Fodera, 2025 NYLJ LEXIS 3543, 2025 LX 552729, the court concluded that the third-party plaintiff’s counsel cited “a non-existent case citation and non-existent quotations . . . as a result of his reliance on [GenAI]” following the third-party plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment. Although the court acknowledged the potential benefits of GenAI, it held that the error “cannot be considered minimal” because attorneys have ethical duties to not make false statements to the court. The court therefore denied the summary judgment motion with prejudice, ordered the third-party plaintiff’s attorney to pay a $2,000 sanction, and ordered the counsel to reimburse the third-party defendants’ legal fees.

name: Bankr. M.D. Ala. – Judge Christopher L. Hawkins
summary: In In re Jackson Hosp. & Clinic, No. 25-30256-CLH, 2025 Bankr. LEXIS 3039 (Bankr. M.D. Ala. Nov. 20, 2025), the court issued an order for an attorney and her law firm (who were representing a creditor in a bankruptcy proceeding) to show cause why they should not be sanctioned for the repeated misuse of GenAI in court filings. Specifically, following the creditor’s filing of a related motion, the court observed that cited regulations “did not stand for the legal propositions” for which they were cited, noted that one attorney in particular had also previously cited caselaw that did not stand for the principle she cited it for, and pointed out that the party’s supporting briefs for a motion to reconsider the court’s decision also “continued to miscite authorities, and [the party’s supplemental brief] even recycled a fabricated quote” from another filing. In response to the court’s show cause order, the law firm conducted an investigation into the offending attorney’s other matters and concluded that she had also included a GenAI-created hallucination in a separate court filing. The attorney eventually admitted that she had “misled the Court” by previously denying the use of GenAI in connection with the filing, when in fact she “was aware [GenAI] was used by someone other than an associate at the Firm.” The court cited Alabama Ethics Rules 1.1, 3.1, and 3.3, 28 U.S.C. § 1927, Bankruptcy Rule 9011, and Bankruptcy Section 105(a), and the court’s inherent authority in concluding that while sanctions were not appropriate for the law firm, “the Court will impose a certification requirement on the Firm” to ensure that it takes further necessary steps to “prevent future abuse” of GenAI. The court did, however, find that sanctions were appropriate against the specific offending attorney, and publicly reprimanded her, ordered her to inform her clients, opposing counsel, and every court in which she is counsel of this opinion within 31 days, revoked the attorney’s pro hac vice status, and ordered the attorney must provide the clerk of court with a listing of jurisdictions in which she is licensed to practice law within 24 hours of the court’s order.
applicableTo: Applies to AI Used for Filings/Drafting

name: E.D. Wash. – Judge Stan Bastian
summary: In Dam v. Waldron (In re Giga Watt Inc.), No. 2:25-CV-00077-SAB, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 228861 (E.D. Wash. Nov. 20, 2025), the court ruled on the parties’ various appellate motions in a bankruptcy proceeding. Appellee asked the court to issue an order for the pro se appellant to show cause why he should not be sanctioned on the grounds that the appellant made misrepresentations and “submitted fabricated legal theory generated by [GenAI].” The court concluded that in light of the appellant’s pro se status, because the court previously dismissed the action in appellee’s favor, and because there were no allegations that that “cases were completely fabricated or otherwise ‘hallucinated’ by AI,” sanctions were not warranted, and the court denied appellee’s motion.
